en: Oṃ. Homage to the Buddha.
The Epic Poem *Saundarananda*,
Canto One: A Description of Kapilavastu.
There was a sage named Kapila Gautama, the best among the upholders of dharma, who,
like Gautama Kākṣīvata, had grown weary from his ascetic penances.
He who constantly resorted to blazing asceticism like Kāśyapa,
and attained supreme perfection in its increase like Kāśyapa.
He who, like Vasiṣṭha, milked the cow for himself from the sacrificial offerings;
and he who, like Vasiṣṭha, milked the cow from his disciples who were perfected through austerity. ||3||
He who, by virtue of his great asceticism, became like a second Dīrghatapas, and who, by his wisdom, was like a third Kāvya-Aṅgiras; ||4||
On the auspicious side of that vast Himavat mountain,
there was a field and a sanctuary which became a hermitage for austerities.
With its beautiful groves of trees and thickets, and its lush, soft,
green meadows, it always appeared like a cloud due to the canopy of sacrificial smoke.
With its soft, sandy, and smooth ground, pale with scattered filaments, and its open spaces, the place appeared as if it were adorned with cosmetic unguents.
It stood as if possessed of kinsmen in the form of lakes filled with lotuses— lakes that were pure, reckoned as sacred fords (tīrtha), purifying, and full of spiritual inspiration.
With rows of forests on all sides filled with fully developed fruits and flowers,
the mountain shone and grew in splendor like a man possessed of effective means.
Though crowded with ascetics contented with wild rice and fruits— self-composed, peaceful, and free from worldly desire— it was as if utterly empty.
There, the sound of sacrificial fires being offered into, of peacocks crying out,
and of holy bathing sites during ablutions was heard.
There, the deer, sleeping upon the pure sacrificial altars,
shone as if they were offerings made with *mādhavī* flowers and parched grain.
Even the small animals there wandered peacefully with the deer,
as if they had learned discipline from the ascetics who provide refuge.
Even though the absence of rebirth was still a matter of doubt and the scriptures were contradictory,
those whose wealth is austerity performed penance there as if they were direct perceivers of the truth.
In this [system], Brahman is measured by some and not measured by others;
Soma is measured at the proper time, and never measured at an improper time. (15)
Indifferent toward their bodies, those ascetics, whose intellects were fixed on the Dharma, practiced austerity with great effort as if they were filled with joy.
There the sages, striving with minds intent on attaining heaven, seemed by their passion for austerity to bring about the very destruction of dharma. ||17||
Then some princes of the Ikṣvāku lineage, desiring to dwell there, went to that hermitage, which was the abode of the radiant and a field of asceticism.
With bodies like pillars of gold, possessing the majesty of lions and mighty arms, they were the worthy recipients of great renown, prosperity, and humility. (19)
For those of noble form are indeed worthy [to rule] over one who is unworthy, the high-souled over one of fickle mind, and the wise over a younger brother who is devoid of wisdom. (20)
They endured the royal splendor that had come to them as their mother’s dowry,
and they protected their father’s truth, which was why they dwelt in the forest.
The sage Kapila Gautama became their preceptor;
thus, because of their teacher's lineage, they who were Kautsas became Gautamas.
Just as two brothers who share the same father become distinct due to their separate acceptance of teachers—
one was Rāma Gārgya and the other was Vāsubhadra Gautama.
Because they made their dwelling concealed by śāka trees, those descendants of Ikṣvāku are known on earth as Śākyas. ||24||
Gautama performed for them rites befitting his own lineage,
just as the sage Bhārgava did for the boy Sagara.
He was like Kaṇva to the energetic Bharata, son of Śakuntalā,
and like the wise Vālmīki to the two wise sons of Maithilī.
That forest, by means of that sage and those preeminent kṣatriyas,
simultaneously bore the splendor of both the Brahmanical and Kṣatriya orders— peaceful and well-guarded.
Then, taking up a water-pot with the desire to bring about their prosperity,
that sage flew up into the sky and spoke to those princes.
"Let that stream which falls from this jar of inexhaustible water reach me in due order, without overstepping it. (29)
Then, having said "So be it" and prostrated with their heads,
they all mounted their well-adorned chariots drawn by swift horses.
Then, followed by them as they stood upon their chariots,
he moved through the sky and sprinkled water over the edge of that hermitage’s grounds.
Having drawn a checkerboard pattern as if with signs that made it fragrant, the sage stood there and spoke thus to those daughters of the king: (32)
"When I have departed for the celestial realm, you must construct a city within this area demarcated by the stream and characterized by the mark of the wheel. (33)
Then, on one occasion, when that sage had departed, those heroes roamed about unrestrained like elephants in the full vigor of their youth.
Wearing leather finger-guards bound upon their hands, with bows grasped in their hands,
great quivers filled with arrows, and their garments tightly girded.
Seeking to test his skill among both serpents and beasts of prey,
they imitated the forest-dwelling son of Duṣyanta, Devakarmā.
Seeing that they had returned to their natural state like aged tiger cubs,
the ascetics abandoned that forest and took refuge on the Himalayas.
Then, seeing that hermitage site empty of them, those whose minds were desolate, tormented by grief, sighed like venomous serpents. (38)
Then those performers of meritorious deeds, whose prosperity was imminent, obtained great treasures described there by those who know them. (39)
Enough with the pursuit of all the aims of dharma, artha, and kāma;
you possess many various kinds of treasures, free from all enemies. (40)
Then, because of the acquisition of that site and the transformation of their past karma, those who were experts in architecture established a glorious city upon that ground. (41)
With moats as wide as rivers and clearly defined, elegant main roads, it possessed great ramparts like unto mountains—resembling another Girivraja. 42.
With its white palaces as its beautiful face and its well-arranged market-stalls,
it was surrounded by rows of mansions like the central valley of the Himalayas.
There, the Brahmins—learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, established in the six duties—recited [the scriptures] for the sake of peace and prosperity. 44.
In that land, by his own power, he caused the servants of those who attacked his territory to refrain from their attacks, thereby restraining them through punishment.
There he stationed worthy householders who were endowed with the wealth of good conduct, possessed of modesty, far-sighted, brave, and skillful. (46)
He appointed those ministers to various corresponding tasks, each endowed with specific qualities such as intelligence, eloquence, and prowess.
It shone, crowded with men who were wealthy, undeluded, highly learned, and free from pride,
like Mount Mandara filled with Kinnaras.
There, with joyful minds and a desire to please the citizens, they established glorious monuments known as gardens, which were abodes of fame. (49)
And by their own volition, not by command, they dug auspicious lotus-pools in all directions, filled with water of the most excellent qualities.
They established everywhere along the roads and in the groves beautiful, glorious, and excellent assembly halls, complete even with wells.
It was crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, yet it was not congested and remained unperturbed;
the wealth of its supplicants was never concealed, while its knowledge and prowess remained hidden.
It was like a storehouse for riches, a receptacle for splendors, an abode for sciences, and a meeting-place for prosperities. (53)

He was a wish-fulfilling tree for the virtuous, a refuge for those seeking shelter, a home for those who had mastered the scriptures, and a tethering post for those endowed with great strength of arm. (54)
With social gatherings, festivals, gifts, and ritual observances, those of immense valor adorned that city, the abode of the world. (55)
Because they did not impose any unjust tax upon anyone,
they filled that city with prosperity in a very short time.
And because they built that city on the site of the hermitage of that seer Kapila, it was therefore called Kapilavāstu.
Just as cities are heard of in the hermitages of Kakanda, Makanda, and Kuśāmba, so too is that [city] of Kapila.
Those sons, resembling Indra in their splendor, entered that city with noble majesty and not with arrogance;
and from that time forth, they were perpetually fragrant with the scent of glory, like the illustrious sons of Yayāti. (59)
Even with princes acting as its lords, the kingdom did not shine, being without a king;
like the sky when the moon has not yet risen, despite thousands of stars shining.
Among those brothers, he who was the eldest by age and in virtues— a bull among bulls in his vigor—
the Ādityas, who hold their preceptor dear, consecrated him there.
Like the thousand-eyed one in heaven. ||61||
Possessed of right conduct, discipline, policy, and ritual action,
he protected the kingdom for the sake of dharma and not for the pleasure of the senses, holding the royal parasol while surrounded by his brothers.
Like Saṃkrandana following after heaven with the Maruts. ||62||
The first canto, titled "Description of Kapilavastu," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is concluded.
The second canto: King Śuddhodana.
Then, after some time, by virtue of his lineage,
there arose a king named Śuddhodana, whose actions were pure and who had conquered his senses.
He who was not attached to sensual pleasures, nor did he marvel at the attainment of prosperity;
he did not despise others for their success, nor did he feel distressed because of others.
He is powerful, endowed with courage, learned, and intelligent;
he is valiant, possessed of political wisdom, steadfast, and indeed of pleasant countenance. (3)
He was handsome yet not arrogant; skillful yet not lacking in uprightness; radiant yet not lacking in patience; and a doer of deeds yet never conceited. ||4||
Though attacked by enemies in battle and sought for refuge by friends,
he never turned his back, owing both to his splendor and his desire to give.
He who, desiring to follow the path of righteousness trodden by former kings,
followed his ancestors in conduct while bearing the burden of the kingdom as if it were a sacred initiation.
Through his excellent administration and protection, the subjects lived in happiness, free from anxiety, as if resting upon the lap of a father. (7)
Whether he had mastered the scriptures or the weapons, or whether he was born into a noble family,
no one who came into his presence was seen to have failed to achieve his purpose.
Though addressed with words that were beneficial yet unpleasant, he listened well and remained undisturbed;
having abandoned even great wrongdoing, he remembered even the smallest good deed.
He showed favor to those who bowed before him; he subdued his enemies;
he protected those in distress; and he restrained those who had strayed from the path.
Generally, those who followed his conduct were seen acquiring virtues just as they acquired wealth. (11)
He studied the supreme Brahman and never wavered from his steadfastness;
he bestowed gifts upon worthy recipients and committed no sin whatsoever.
With fortitude, he upheld his vow like a noble steed bearing its yoke;
for he did not desire life even for a moment once he had fallen away from truth.
He attended upon the learned, shone forth through his self-possession,
and gleamed before the disciplined like the moon in its fullness.
Through both his intellect and his study of the scriptures, he understood what was appropriate for this world and the next;
and through his fortitude and valor, he protected both his senses and his subjects.
He took away the suffering of the distressed and the exalted glory of his enemies; and by means of his statesmanship, he acquired both the earth and even greater fame.
By nature compassionate, he felt sorrow upon seeing those who were suffering;
nor did he pursue fame out of greed by means of wealth acquired through unjust ways. (17)

Because of his firm devotion born of affection, he did not fail to give each of his friends their respective wealth according to their needs, even when they were devoid of merit, owing to his benevolent disposition.
Without having first offered the best portion to the Arhats, he did not eat anything, nor did he drink water;
he did not milk the cow by means of unrighteousness, as one might milk a cow out of a thirst for milk.

He did not consume an offering that had not been brought forward, nor did he ascend to the heights of pride or sovereign power; he sharpened his intellect through the sacred scriptures for the sake of dharma, and not for the sake of fame.
Yet he did not afflict even those who were worthy of his affliction with defiled actions; nor, because of his noble nature, did he fail to perceive the virtues even of his enemies. (21)
Like the moon, he drew the eyes of the people toward him with his physical form;
yet on this earth, he did not covet the property of others, as one would avoid a highly venomous serpent.
No one anywhere was harmed by anyone within his domain;
for he commanded that the bow held in his hand grant fearlessness to those in distress.
He looked with an affectionate gaze even upon those who had committed offenses when they bowed before him, let alone those who had previously done him kindness; he refreshed them with gentle words.
He acquired many branches of knowledge while remaining free from curiosity regarding sense-objects;
established in the dharma of the Kṛta age, he did not falter from righteousness even in times of hardship.
He constantly increased in virtues and grew through the excellence of his friends;
he remained steadfast among the elders and did not turn toward a censurable path.
He quelled his enemies with arrows, delighted his kinsmen with virtues, did not incite his servants through vulnerabilities, and did not oppress the subjects with taxes. ||27||
Through protection and through valor, he sowed the entire earth;
and by means of a transparent system of governance, he caused the sacrificial sessions of the night to flourish.
By the conduct of a royal seer, he caused the fragrance of fame to grow in his lineage;
with his brilliance, he drove away darkness, just as the sun dispels it with its splendor.
He caused his ancestors to expand through virtues equal to those of a virtuous son, and he gladdened his subjects with his conduct, as a cloud refreshes them with water.
Through constant and extensive gifts, he caused the Soma to flow for the Brahmins;
and by abiding in the duties of a king, he caused the crops to ripen in due season.
He, who was free from doubt, spoke no discourse that was unrighteous;
and like a universal monarch, he overcame his enemies for the sake of dharma.
He did not diminish the kingdom or his army in any way;
rather, through his very servants, he vigorously shattered the pride of his enemies.
By his own virtues alone, he caused his lineage to flourish ever more and more;
yet, through the orderly establishment of all duties, he never allowed his subjects to perish.
Unwearied, the sacrificer performed his rites at the proper time and measured out the sacrificial ground;
and by protecting the twice-born, he caused the Veda to flourish without anxiety.
At the proper time, he duly caused the gentle Soma to be measured out by his preceptors;
and through his ascetic power and splendor, he caused the army of his enemies to be destroyed.
The knower of the supreme dharma caused his subjects to dwell in the subtle dharma;
and through the very vision of dharma, he caused them to dwell in heaven at the proper time.
Even though he was clearly capable, he did not appoint an unrighteous man to difficult tasks;
nor did he, out of mere affection, promote one who was incompetent simply because he was dear to him. (38)
With his splendor and brilliance, he caused his arrogant enemies to tremble;
and with his blazing lamp of fame, he caused the entire earth to tremble.
Out of consideration for the benefits [to others], and not for the sake of fame, he gave to the seeker; and even after relinquishing great wealth, he incurred no infamy whatsoever.
Therefore, even an enemy who had come for refuge was not abandoned by him, though he was afflicted by suffering;
nor did he feel pride after conquering even haughty foes. (41)
He did not transgress the bounds of propriety out of desire, hatred, or even fear;
therefore, although enjoyments were present, he did not indulge in the habitual functioning of his senses. (42)
He never perceived any task as difficult anywhere;
nor did he ever fail in action when it came to performing what was unpleasant or pleasant. (43)
Accordingly, he drank the Soma and attained fame as prescribed by the ritual;
he constantly studied the Veda and practiced the dharma declared in the Veda. (44)
Thus, by means of such qualities that were difficult to find, that Śākya king—though surrounded by vassal lords who were themselves powerful—became invincible, like Śakra himself. (45)
Then, at that time, the gods, desiring righteousness and wishing to behold the practice of dharma, wandered through the quarters of the world.
Wandering through the world with a desire to know dharma, those whose souls were devoted to dharma beheld that king, who was especially devoted to dharma.
Then the Bodhisattva, descending from the Tuṣita gods to the earth,
made a vow for rebirth in the family of that lord of the earth.
At that time, that queen of the god-like king was named Māyā;
she was free from anger, darkness, and illusion, like the goddess Māyā herself in heaven. (49)
Then, at that time, she saw in a dream a white six-tusked elephant entering her womb, possessing power like that of Airāvata. (50)
Having heard that dream, the twice-born experts in dreams explained it to him as portending the birth of a prince who would be the bearer of fortune, virtue, and glory. (51)
When that distinguished being was born—one who sought the destruction of birth—the earth, though immovable, trembled like a boat struck by waves. (52)
An unblemished rain of flowers fell from the sky, as if shaken from the Caitraratha grove by the trunks of the elephants of the quarters, or stirred by the rays of the sun.
In the sky, the kettledrums resounded like those of the sporting Maruts;
the sun shone with exceeding brilliance, and an auspicious breeze blew. (54)
The Tuṣita and Śuddhāvāsa deities were indeed filled with joy, out of great reverence for the True Dharma and out of compassion for sentient beings. (55)
The supreme one, who brings about the banner of welfare, approached Yaśaḥketu;
he shone with peaceful splendor like Dharma incarnate.
To the younger queen, Araṇyā, a son named Nanda was born, who brought eternal joy to the family, just as fire is born in the forest.
Long-armed, broad-chested, with shoulders like a lion’s and eyes like a bull’s,
he who by his preeminent form truly bore the epithet "Sundara" (the Handsome One).
Like the month of Madhu arrived, like the moon newly risen,
and like the bodiless god of love endowed with limbs, he shone with lovely splendor.
The lord of men brought them up with supreme joy,
just as great wealth held in the hands of a virtuous person fosters both dharma and desire.
In the course of time, those two noble sons grew up for his welfare,
just as virtue and worldly prosperity increase for the benefit of a noble man who undertakes great endeavors.
Between those two virtuous sons, that King of the Śākyas shone resplendent,
like the Middle Country clearly situated between the Himavat and Pāriyātra mountains.
Then, after those two sons of the king had been consecrated and had gradually mastered their learning,
Nanda took constant delight in sensual pleasures, but Sarvārthasiddha felt no attachment to them.
Having beheld the aged, the afflicted, and the dead, and reflecting upon the world’s ignorance, his heart was filled with distress;
possessed of compassion for others dwelling within his own heart, he found no delight in the objects of the senses, desiring to utterly destroy the fear of birth and death on all sides. (64)
Out of world-weariness, having fixed his mind on non-rebirth,
he departed from the royal palace at night— indifferent to the sleeping, beautiful women and intent on going to the forest— like a *kalahaṃsa* swan leaving a lake where the lotuses have been crushed.
The second canto, titled "Description of the King," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The third canto: "Description of the Tathāgata."

Then, having abandoned Kapilavastu—which was crowded with throngs of horses, elephants, and chariots, magnificent, and inhabited by people devoted to him through fearlessness—he, his mind resolved, went to the forest for the sake of asceticism. (1)

Having observed those sages who followed various scriptures and resorted to diverse disciplines of austerity, yet were wretched in their thirst for sense-objects, he turned away from that unstable form of asceticism. ||2||

Then, having attended upon Ārāḍa, who taught liberation, as well as Udraka, whose mind was set on tranquility, he—whose intellect was fixed on reality and who was skilled in the path—declared: "I too have abandoned this non-path. (3)
Reflecting upon what might be supreme in the world, he examined various scriptures;
failing to attain certainty, he practiced even more difficult asceticism under another teacher.
Then, perceiving that "this is not the path," he abandoned even that extensive austerity;
having understood the supreme object of meditation, he partook of excellent food for the sake of attaining immortality.
With arms like a pair of golden pillars, with the gait of a bull and long eyes,
he approached a Plakṣa tree for the desire to know the supreme method of ascetic discipline.
Having sat there with a firm resolve and unshakable fortitude like the king of mountains,
he then conquered the fierce army of Māra and awakened to the auspicious, supreme, and imperishable state.

And having understood that he had accomplished his task, the gods, their minds set on immortality, attained a joy beyond compare; yet the assembly of Māra, turning away from them, was agitated with distress. ||8||
The earth with its mountains trembled, and Śiva, the friend of fire, blew a favorable breeze;
the celestial drums resounded, and the sky, though free of clouds, rained down.
Having realized the supreme truth that is ageless, the All-pervading Lord, out of compassion,
went to the city surrounded by Varanasi in order to demonstrate the eternal immortality.

Then, for the welfare of the world, the Sage turned there in the assembly the Wheel of Dharma, whose hub is the Deathless, whose rim is steadfastness, intelligence, and concentration, and whose spokes are discipline and restraint. (11)
"Thus, this is suffering; this is its proliferating creeper of origination;
this is peace; and this is the means"—this supreme tetrad is distinguished according to its specific divisions. (12)
And having proclaimed the peerless, irreversible, and supreme Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects, the Seer first instructed him who belonged to the Kauṇḍinya lineage.

For he crossed over the unfathomable ocean of faults—whose waters are the acquisitions (upadhi), whose creatures are mental afflictions (ādhi), and which is stirred by the waves of anger, pride, and fear—and he caused the world to cross as well. (14)
Having disciplined many people among the Kāśis, the Gayas, and then at Giri-vraja, that one of supreme compassion then went to his father’s city out of a desire to show them favor. (15)
For Gautama, whose body was like the sun, arose and dispelled the darkness, just as the sun does, for those people who are devoted to sense-objects and follow many various paths.
Then, with a mind free from desire, he beheld Kapilavastu on all sides— a city celebrated for its most auspicious foundations— dwelling in which was exceedingly pure, like a forest of sacred groves.
For he had become one who possessed nothing, his mind fixed in restraint and finding his lordship within the self;
how much less, then, could he have attachment for kinsmen, people of his own country, friends, or material objects—all of which produce manifold fears? (18)

He did not rejoice at being honored, nor did he fall into grief through contempt; firm in his resolve, he underwent no change of state toward either the sword or sandalwood, nor toward suffering and pleasure.
Then the king, having learned that his son had approached the Tathāgata, set out quickly with only a few horses following him, out of an eager desire to see his son. ||20||
The Sugata, having looked upon the Tathāgata— the king who was lacking in resolve due to his longing—
and desiring to lead even the remaining people whose faces were bathed in tears, flew up into the sky.
He strode across heaven as if over the earth; having stood still, he sat down again;
with an unwavering mind, he lay down; then he became manifold, and again he became one.
He moved upon the water as if on land, he entered the earth as if it were water;
like a cloud he rained down repeatedly in the sky, and like the newly risen sun, he blazed with radiance.
Blazing simultaneously like a fire and discharging water like a cloud,
he shone with a luster resembling molten gold, like a cloud illuminated by the twilight.
Beholding that banner, which rose up as if encircled by a network of gold and jewels, the king attained incomparable joy, and the prostrate people offered him great respect. (25)
Then, perceiving that the lord of men had been made a fit vessel by his perfection of supernatural power,
and that the city folk were likewise inclined toward him, the Guide proclaimed the discipline of the Dharma.
Then the king first obtained the fruit for the sake of accomplishing the dharma of immortality;
having attained incomparable dharma from the sage, he bowed to the sage as if to a guru. (27)
Then many who were of serene mind, fearing the afflictions of birth and death, those successful bulls among the Śākya sons, went forth like bulls fleeing from the fear of fire. (28)

But even those who did not abandon their homes out of regard for their children, fathers, and mothers, they too, with disciplined minds, undertook the rules of restraint and maintained them until death. (29)

They did not harm even the smallest creature, though they lived by the slaughter of others; how much less, then, one of noble birth, possessed of great virtues, always compassionate, and devoted to the service of a sage? (30)

Though his efforts were unwearied and his wealth meager, and though he could not endure the insults of others, he did not seize the riches of another; for he trembled at the wealth of others as if it were a venomous serpent. (31)

Although he was endowed with wealth, though he was young, and though his senses were restless for sense-objects, he never approached the wives of others; for he regarded them as more burning than fire itself.
No one spoke an untruth, nor did anyone utter even the truth if it was unpleasant;
no one spoke even a gentle word that was not beneficial, nor did anyone say anything that was beneficial but derived from malice. (33)
He was never seduced by his mind toward the wealth of others, nor did he have a greedy heart;
reflecting upon sensual pleasure as being non-pleasure, that virtuous man lived there as if already satisfied. (34)
Furthermore, being compassionate, he did not even contemplate causing harm to another;
for there, the people regarded one another as they would their own mother, father, son, or friend. (35)

He attained the correct vision that the fruit of karma will certainly exist in the future, as well as in the present and the past; furthermore, he understood that the destiny of beings in the world is likewise determined. (36)
Thus, by means of these ten kinds of vast and supremely virtuous deeds,
the people there lived in that declining age— even though its virtues had grown lax— by taking refuge in the Sage.
And yet, because of those virtues, no one there desired the happiness of rebirth;
having realized that existence is entirely inauspicious, they turned toward the destruction of existence, not toward further birth. (38)
Even householders, free from doubt and possessing supremely pure vision, entered the stream; indeed, many did so, while others even brought about the thinning of the dust of passion. (39)

Even those who were here engaged in sense-objects corresponding to their wealth, though devoted to renunciation, humility, and self-restraint, wandered about yet did not deviate from the path of the righteous. (40)
Moreover, there was no fear from oneself, nor from others, nor from fate;
and in that Kṛta Age, the subjects rejoiced in the qualities of great happiness and abundant food, as if in the time of Manu.
Thus that city became joyful, free from disease, and devoid of calamity— resembling the cities of the Kurus, the Raghus, and the Puru dynasty—
while the Great Sage, the teacher of fearlessness, dwelt there for its welfare, having transcended all passion.
The third canto, titled "Description of the Tathāgata," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
Canto Four: The Request for His Wife.

But even while the sage was speaking there of dharma, and while his kinsmen remained indifferent toward dharma, Nanda—dwelling in his palace, devoted solely to the pursuit of pleasure, and accompanied by his beloved—continued to enjoy himself. (1)
For, united with that beloved wife as a male ruddy goose is with his mate,
he who was worthy of love did not think of Vaiśravaṇa nor of Śakra for the sake of their status, much less of Dharma.

She was addressed by three names: she was called *Sundarī* because of her fortune and her beauty; *Māninī* because of her steadfastness and her pride; and *Bhāminī* because of her radiance and her dignity. (3)
That woman-lotus, with her laughter for swans, her eyes for bees, and her full breasts for lofty lotus buds,
shone once more through the sun that delighted her— her own kinsman who had arisen.
With a form exceedingly captivating and with movements corresponding to that form, she was indeed at that time the most beautiful woman among women and Nanda among men in the world of humans. (5)
That goddess was like one wandering in the Nandana grove, and Nanda was the bringer of joy to his family;
they appeared as if created by the Sustainer of Beings, surpassing mortals yet not reaching the level of gods.

If Nanda does not obtain that Sundarī, or if she of the arched brows does not attend upon him, then that couple will surely not shine, being incomplete like the night and the moon deprived of one another. (7)
He took as his wife that pair who were like the targets of Love and Passion, the nesting place of joy and bliss, and the vessel of exultation and contentment—blinded by intoxication. (8)
With eyes intent on gazing at one another, with minds attached to each other’s speech, and with the body-unguents removed by their mutual embrace—that couple captivated one another. (9)
Both of them, devoted to one another and dwelling by a mountain torrent like a kinnarī and a kiṃpuruṣa,
played and shone with the splendor of their beauty, as if vying with each other.
By increasing their mutual passion, that couple delighted one another;
in the intervals of fatigue, by amusing one another, they joyfully intoxicated one another with playfulness.
Then, desiring to serve his beloved, he adorned her, yet not for the sake of mere decoration;
for she, already adorned by her own natural beauty, was the ornament even of ornaments. (12)
Then, placing a mirror in his hand, she said to her beloved, "Hold this for a moment before me while I apply my forehead mark," and he held it for her.
Then, observing her husband’s beard, she applied a decorative mark upon it that was exactly like his own;
and Nanda, having cured the mirror with the breath of his sighs, struck it down. (14)
She laughed inwardly at her husband’s playful gestures and his deceit;
yet, as if she were indeed angry with him, she knit her brows in a frown upon her forehead. (15)
With his left hand, languid with intoxication, he cast a *karṇotpala* flower upon his shoulder;
then, with its petals as fingers, he pressed that very same flower against his face, whose eyes were half-closed.

Then Nanda, out of fear, bowed his head at the feet of his beloved; her feet were adorned with jingling anklets, their toes were illuminated by the luster of her nails, and they possessed the radiance of lotuses.

Then, with his head adorned by the blossoming flowers he had released, that doer of what was dear to his beloved shone like a *nāga* tree on a golden altar, its branches bent down by the wind as if from the excessive weight of its flowers. (18)
With the pearl necklace displaced from her breasts, she raised him up, pressing him with both arms;
and with her earrings tilted as she turned her face, she laughed loudly, asking, "How have you become like this? (19)
Then, repeatedly looking at her husband’s face as his hand rested upon the mirror,
she completed that decorative mark on her cheek, which was moist with *tamāla* paste.

Her face, with its tamāla-leaf ornament, copper-colored lower lip, and eyes as long as her hair, shone like a lotus with its stalk still attached, its tips reddened by pollen, and a bee alighting upon it. ||21||
Then Nanda, respectfully holding a mirror as a witness to her adornment,
with eyes squinting to examine the decorative patterns, gazed at his beloved’s face as she playfully flirted.
Beholding his beloved’s face—beautiful with its distinctive mark bitten by her earrings, like a lotus bruised by a *kāraṇḍava* duck—Nanda became even more a bringer of joy to his beloved. (23)
Then, within the interior of that celestial palace in the Vimānakalpa, Nanda rejoiced in that very manner;
and the Tathāgata, at the time when alms were due, entered his house for the sake of alms.
With his face cast down and without offering a greeting, he remained in his brother's house just as if he were in the house of a stranger;
then, due to the negligence of the servants, he departed again without having received any alms.
One woman ground fragrant unguents for the body, while another perfumed her garments;
likewise, one prepared the ritual for bathing, and others wove fragrant garlands.
In that house, while performing their graceful duties suited to play with their husbands, some young women did not perceive the Buddha; for this was surely the intention of the Buddha.

But a certain woman standing there on the roof of the palace, having fixed her eye toward the opening of a window, beheld the Sugata emerging like the blazing sun from within the womb of a cloud. (28)
Having considered the respect due to her husband and her own devotion toward the Arhat, she stood before Nanda, desiring to speak; and by his permission, she then related this: (29)
I suspect that the Blessed One has entered our house as a teacher to show favor to these people;
for, failing to receive alms, speech, or a seat, he departs once more like from a desolate forest. (30)
Hearing that the great seer had entered his house and was departing again without receiving honors,
he— adorned with variegated ornaments, garments, and garlands like a wish-fulfilling tree— trembled as if shaken by the wind.
Then, placing his lotus-like hands joined in reverence upon his head, he requested his beloved to go with him, saying:
"I shall go to pay my respects to my teacher; you ought to grant me permission to depart. (32)
Trembling, she embraced him like a creeper shaken by the wind;
and with eyes rolling and flooded with tears, she sighed deeply and spoke these words. (33)
"I ought not to cause you, who are desirous of going to see your father, any hindrance to your dharma.
Go, noble son, and return very quickly, before this cosmetic mark has dried. (34)
If you were indeed to be procrastinating, I would inflict a great punishment upon you;
I would wake you from your sleep with my breasts again and again, yet I would not speak to you. (35)
Moreover, if you approach me while my body is still fresh and unwithered, then I shall quickly crush you with my two arms— arms now stripped of ornaments yet still moist with unguents.
Thus addressed and pressed by her, whose voice was discordant with her appearance, he said:
"I shall do so; release me, O fierce one, before that teacher of mine has gone far away. (37)
Then, released from her arms— which were smeared with sandalwood paste from her breasts— but not from her heart,
he cast off his attire suited to love and assumed a form worthy of honor.
As her lover departed, she brooded over him, her eyes fixed and motionless in the vacancy of deep thought;
with ears pricked up and her mouth agape as if grazing on grass, she stood like a doe whose prey has fled.
With his mind drawn away by the desire to see the sage, Nanda hastened toward his departure;
yet, turning his gaze back, he proceeded slowly, looking at her as an elephant looks at a playful female elephant.

Gazing with a sidelong glance at that beautiful woman, whose waist was slender and whose breasts and thighs were full— resembling a golden cave in a mountain— Nanda was not satiated, as if he were drinking water with only one hand.
That reverence directed toward the Buddha drew him forward, while his love for his wife drew him back;
due to this indecision, he neither went nor stayed, like a royal swan tossed upon the waves.
Having lost sight of her, he descended quickly from that palace;
yet, upon hearing the sound of her anklets, his heart was seized and he hung back once more. (43)
Held back by his passion for sensual desires and drawn forward by his love for the Dharma, he proceeded with difficulty, being turned back like a boat on a river going against the current. (44)
Then he set out with very long strides, thinking, "How indeed might my pace not be heavy?
and "How might I embrace that beloved, who so cherished her forehead-mark, while her mark was still wet? (45)
Then, on the road, he saw the Daśabala— who had cast off pride even in his father’s city and was likewise free from self-conceit—
stopping nearby, like the honored banner of Indra being followed by a procession.
The fourth canto, titled "The Borrowed Wife," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The fifth canto: Nanda’s Ordination.

Then, having dismounted from their horses, chariots, and elephants, the Śākyas, each assuming attire according to his own rank, and the merchants from the great marketplaces, bowed out of devotion to the Great Sage. ||1||
Some, having bowed, followed for a moment; some, having bowed, departed according to their business;
others remained in their own dwellings with palms joined, their eyes fixed intently upon his gaze. ||2||
Then, on that royal road, the Buddha proceeded with difficulty through the great stream of devoted people,
like a river’s current during the rainy season struggling against its own torrent.
Then Nanda was unable to offer his salutation to the Tathāgata, who was being thus honored by the great ones as they flocked together; yet he took delight in the majesty of his Teacher.
Desiring to cast off his own attachment on the road, protecting the devotion of the people toward another teacher,
and wishing to win over Nanda who was intent on returning home, the Sugata then took a different path.
Then Nanda, his mind secluded and knowing the true path, set out upon the solitary way;
having gone before him, he bowed to that most excellent one who was liberated through joy.

Advancing slowly with reverence, his shoulders covered by his robe, his body bent low, with his hands joined palm-to-palm below and his eyes cast upward, he spoke these words in a faltering voice: (7)
Standing upon the palace roof, I heard that the Blessed One had entered within to bestow his grace;
therefore, filled with haste and feeling a sense of envy toward the great courtyard of the house, I have approached. (8)
Therefore, O beloved of the virtuous, it is well; for my sake, O best of monks, let this be the time for alms there.
For the sun, desiring to go toward the meridian of the sky, seems indeed to be reminding me of the hour. (9)
Thus addressed by him who was prostrate before him, his eyes upturned with affectionate pride,
the Sugata performed such a miraculous sign that he understood there would be no need for food.
Then, having prostrated before the sage, he set his mind on departing for home;
but the Sugata, whose eyes were like lotus petals, gave him his alms-bowl as a mark of favor. (11)
Then, for the sake of the fruit of giving in this world, he, being self-restrained, received with his lotus-like hands— capable of grasping a bow— the vessel of that peerless worthy recipient.

Perceiving from afar that the Sugata was turning away with his mind elsewhere and no longer intent on him, Nanda—though holding the alms-bowl in his hand and desiring to go home—turned back from the path, gazing at the Sage. (13)
When he, out of affection for his wife, was desirous of departing even while holding his alms-bowl,
the sage then bewildered him by blocking the entrance of the street.

For the Sage perceived that Nanda possessed the seed of liberation, yet his knowledge was weak while the dust of the afflictions was intense; since he was inclined toward the afflictions and centered on sense objects, the Sage drew him away. (15)
The side of affliction is seen to be twofold, and likewise the side of purification is of two kinds:
that which has the self as its basis for one who emphasizes the power of causes, and that which has the external as its basis for one who values conditions. (16)
But one who possesses superior causal power through effortlessness is liberated at the very moment of being struck;
whereas one whose intellect is led by conditions through effort attains liberation by means of another's support. //17//
And Nanda, whose mind was led by faith, attained a state of identity with him whom he had taken as his refuge;
for the Sage, wishing to lift him out from the mire of affection, provided him with that food there.
But Nanda, struggling with grief, followed his elder brother slowly and helplessly,
reflecting upon the face of his wife, with its eyes restless in gazing and its decorative marks still fresh.
Then the sage led him— whose garlands and necklaces were dear to him, who had come with the month of spring,
and whose pleasure-groves for women were broken— to a monastery that was esteemed as a playground for knowledge.
Then the Greatly Compassionate One, seeing him so wretched, felt pity for a moment;
he touched the man’s head with his hand, which bore the mark of the wheel on its palm, and spoke this to him: ||21||
O gentle one, as long as the destructive time has not yet arrived, apply your mind to tranquility;
for death strikes down with its full assault anyone who remains here in any state whatsoever. (22)
Restrain the fickle mind from the insubstantial pleasures of desire, which are common to all and resemble a dream;
for there is no satisfaction for the world through desires, just as there is none for fire fanned by the wind through offerings of oblations. (23)

The wealth of faith is the most excellent among all forms of wealth; the savor of wisdom is the best among all flavors; the bliss of the inner self is the foremost among all pleasures; and the delight in ignorance is the most painful among all sorrows. (24)
He is the most excellent speaker of what is beneficial among friends; he possesses the virtue of endurance for the sake of Dharma among labors;
his supreme duty is for the sake of knowledge among actions—why then should he submit to the slavery of the senses? (25)
Therefore, choose that which is certain, free from fear, grief, and suffering, independent of others, and unassailable by any;
choose that which is eternal, auspicious, and the bliss of peace. Why endure misfortune for the sake of the objects of the senses? (26)
There is no impurity for living beings equal to old age; there is no misfortune in the world equal to disease;
there is no fear on earth equal to death. Indeed, these three must be endured against one's will. (27)
There is no bond equal to affection; there is no stream as captivating as craving;
likewise, there is no fire equal to the fire of passion. If these three do not exist, then you possess happiness.
Separation from loved ones is inevitable, and sorrow resulting from it is certain to be experienced;
even other royal sages, having fallen into madness through grief, wandered about helplessly. (29)
Therefore, don the armor made of wisdom; for the arrows of sorrow cannot prevail over one who is subdued by patience.
Kindle your own inner fire like a small flame, so as to burn away the great thicket of existence. (30)
Just as one who possesses knowledge and holds medicinal herbs in his hand cannot be bitten by any serpent,
so too one who is free from worldly attachment and has conquered the delusion of the world cannot be bitten by the serpent of sorrow.

Having established himself in yoga and fully realized the truth, he does not experience terror at the time of death, like a hero standing in battle with armor fastened, a fine bow in hand, and weapons prepared, desiring victory. (32)
Thus addressed by the Tathāgata, who has compassion for all living beings, Nanda—bold in speech yet sinking in his heart—said "So be it" to the Sugata. (33)
Then, wishing to rescue him from negligence and considering him a worthy vessel for the tradition, the Great Seer, with a benevolent mind, said to Ānanda: "Ordain Nanda for the sake of peace. (34)
Then the sage of Videha said to Nanda, who was weeping within his heart, "Come here.
Thereupon Nanda approached him slowly and said, "I shall not go forth into the religious life. (35)
Having heard that desire of Nanda, the sage of Videha informed the Buddha;
and having ascertained from him as well the state of Nanda’s mind, the great sage spoke to Nanda once more.

O you who have not conquered your self, when I, your elder brother, had gone forth into the religious life, and our brothers followed us, did your mind feel no remorse upon seeing us—your kinsmen—now observing vows while remaining householders? Or is it that you feel no remorse at all? (37)
Those royal seers are surely not unknown to you, who, laughing, took refuge in the forests;
having spat out their desires and longing for peace, they were never thus attached to these miserable pleasures. (38)

Having repeatedly observed the faults in households and having perceived the happiness found in renouncing them, your mind has no desire at all to leave your home, just as the mind of one wishing to die does not wish to leave a land beset by calamities. (39)

O Śiva, how can you have no desire to ascend that very path upon which you are being set forth, like a merchant who has strayed from his caravan while being led back to it? For you are one whose destination is the wilderness of saṃsāra. (40)

He who would lie down out of delusion while his house is burning on all sides and does not flee from it—he would be a negligent man in a world set ablaze by the fire of time, whose flames are disease and old age. (41)

Just as a condemned man being led to his execution might laugh and prattle in his intoxication, so too one who is led toward death while death stands before him with noose in hand is pitiable, heedless, and perverted in mind. (42)
When kings and householders alike—having abandoned their kinsmen and possessions—have gone, will go, and are indeed going away, how can there be any attachment to these impermanent dear ones? (43)
I do not see anything in which pleasure does not become suffering through its transformation into something else;
therefore, attachment to anything is not justified, for if it were justified, there would be no sorrow when that thing passes away. (44)

Therefore, O gentle one, having understood this flickering world to be like an illusion, a painting, or a magician’s trick, abandon the snare of delusion called "the beloved," if your mind intends to cut through the web of suffering. (45)
Better is food that is unpleasant yet results in future welfare than that which is delicious but followed by harm;
for this reason, I urge you toward the auspicious and pure path, even though it is disagreeable.

Just as a nurse restrains a child and extracts a clod of earth that has entered his mouth, so indeed, desiring to pull out the thorn of passion, I have spoken harsh words to you for your own benefit. (47)
Just as a physician restrains a patient and administers even an unpleasant medicine,
so too have I spoken this which is contrary to your wishes, yet it is for your benefit and intended as a favor.

Therefore, as long as this convergence of moments has not yet met with death, and as long as your age is capable of the practice of yoga, apply your intellect to that which is most beneficial during this very time. (49)
Thus addressed by the compassionate Vināyaka, who desired his welfare, Nanda said:
"O Blessed One, I shall do everything according to your word, exactly as you command. (50)
Then the sage of Videha took hold of him as he struggled and embraced him;
with eyes overflowing with tears, he untied the beauty of his hair from that head which resembled a royal parasol. (51)
Then his face, with tears upon it as his hair was being shaved off,
shone like a lotus in a pond whose stalk and tip are bent down when drenched by the rainwater.
Then Nanda, his garments dyed with tree-bark decoctions, overcome by anxiety like a newly captured lordly elephant,
appeared like the full moon at the end of the night when it has entered the dark fortnight and is bathed in the morning glow.
The fifth canto, titled "The Initiation of Nanda," in the *Saundarananda* poem is completed.
The sixth canto: "The Lamentation for His Wife."
Then, when her husband had been taken away by Gaurava and Arati had been overcome by Prīti,
that very Sundarī, remaining right there upon the palace roof, shone forth at that time.
Waiting for her husband’s arrival, she leaned out from the palace roof toward the window, supported by her breasts;
facing the door, she hung there with her face turned sideways, her earrings dangling.
With her necklace dangling and her earrings swaying,
she appeared from that celestial chariot like the most excellent of Apsarases, fallen from her vimāna due to the exhaustion of her ascetic merit, gazing longingly at her beloved.
With her forehead perspiring from exhaustion, her cosmetic paste dried up by her sighs,
and her eyes unsteady with anxiety, she stood there, suspecting her husband of being elsewhere.
Then, from the exhaustion of remaining there so long, she fell right there upon the couch;
she lay across it, her necklace scattered, with one foot still lingering in a single sandal.
Then, a certain woman there, unable to bear the sight of her weeping and sorrowful state,
suddenly began to cry out as she ran down the palace stairs on foot.
Upon hearing the sound of footsteps on the stairs, she immediately sprang up again;
and as if immersed in joy, she rejoiced, suspecting the arrival of her beloved.
Terrifying the pigeons perched in the eaves with the sound of her anklets,
she rushed up the stairs in her joy, unconcerned that the hem of her silk garment had slipped off.
Having seen that woman and being deceived once more, she sighed and returned to her bed;
with her face turned pale, she did not shine, like the sky at the onset of winter when the moon has lost its luster.
Afflicted by the sight of her husband’s absence, burning with both desire and anger,
she sat down with her face resting in her hands and crossed the river of anxiety whose waters were made of grief.
Her face, a rival to the lotus, rested upon her hand which was copper-red like a young sprout;
it shone above the reflected lotus in the water like a lotus bent down over its own reflection.

That woman, reflecting according to her feminine nature— even though her husband was present before her, full of affection as seen and devoted to righteousness— failing to perceive the truth, imagined various things and lamented in various ways.
"Thinking, 'I shall come back to you when the special marks of your face are no longer withered,' he made that promise to me;
for what reason, then, has my beloved—who was ever true to his promise—now become false to his word? (13)

How can this unprecedented transformation have come upon the noble and virtuous one, whose nature is compassion, who is eternally afraid of me, and who is exceedingly generous—could it be due to his own lack of affection or some transgression on my part? (14)

Surely the heart of my beloved, who delights in pleasure and follows my will, has become dispassionate; for even if he still possessed passion, he would not have failed to come had he been a protector of my heart. (15)
Surely another woman, superior to me in beauty, character, and charm, has been seen by my beloved;
for it was after bestowing her empty consolations upon me that he departed, leaving me behind while I was still clinging to him. (16)
"His devotion toward the Buddha was such that his statement to depart was merely a pretext for me;
for if he had truly felt affection for the Sage, he would have feared untruth as he would terrible death. (17)

If he, having taken up the mirror while I was adorning myself with my mind elsewhere for the sake of service, should now hold it for another person, then let there be salutation to that man of fickle friendship! 18.
Those who do not wish to encounter such grief as this ought not to place their trust in men;
for where was his former devotion toward me, and where now is this abandonment, like that of a common person, in a mere instant? (19)
Thus, being separated from her beloved and suspecting him of being with another, she spoke;
then that woman, having ascended his agitated celestial chariot, addressed these words to her with tears. (20)

Even though he is young, handsome, and endowed with good fortune, prosperity, and noble birth—if he has never before behaved affectionately toward you, then he will turn out otherwise; do not be so distressed. (21)
Do not find fault with your husband, for he is dear to you, worthy of your affection, and a doer of what is pleasing to you;
he knows no woman other than you, just as the ruddy goose knows no mate other than his own female partner.
Desiring to dwell at home for your sake and wishing to live for the purpose of pleasing you, he was indeed ordained by his noble brother, the Tathāgata, with his face wet with tears. (23)
Then, having heard that news regarding her husband, she suddenly sprang up with trembling limbs;
clasping her arms, she cried out loudly like a female elephant struck in the heart by a poisoned arrow.

With eyes bloodshot from weeping and rage, her slender body trembling with the agitation of grief, she fell down like a mango branch broken by the excessive weight of its fruit, her string of pearls shattered and disarrayed. ||25||

Clad in a garment of ruby-red hue, with a lotus-like face and eyes as broad as lotus petals, she— once like the goddess Padmā, now fallen from her lotus-throne like the goddess Lakṣmī herself— withered away like a garland of lotuses under the scorching sun.
Reflecting again and again upon the virtues of her husband, she sighed deeply and grew faint;
she shook her forearm, which was adorned with the beauty of ornaments, and her copper-colored fingertips.
"Ornaments serve no purpose for me now," she said, and she cast her jewelry in all directions;
falling there without her ornaments, she shone like a creeper with its clusters of flowers scattered.
Thinking, "This was held by my beloved," she embraced the gold-handled mirror;
and with effort, as if angry, she rubbed her cheeks—which were adorned with tamāla leaves—when they were boldly touched.
Like a female ruddy goose whose mate had been wounded by the tip of a hawk’s wing, she cried out piteously,
as if vying with the pigeons perched upon the palaces who cooed with throats agitated by their warbling.
Though lying upon a costly couch with golden limbs and feet, adorned with lapis lazuli and diamonds and spread with various soft coverlets, she found no peace as she tossed about.
Beholding her husband’s ornaments, garments, the lute, and other playthings,
she entered into darkness, wailed aloud, and sank down as if fallen into a mire.
With her belly heaving from her sighs, that beautiful woman was like a cave in a mountain split open by a thunderbolt fire;
burning within her heart with the fire of grief, she then became as if her mind were utterly distraught. ||33||
She wept, grew faint, cried out, withered away, wandered about, stood still, lamented, and brooded;
she displayed her anger, scattered her garlands, scratched her face, and tore at her garment. (34)
Hearing that Cārudantī was weeping so violently, the women were deeply distressed;
out of terror, they ascended from the inner apartments to the palace roof, like Kinnarīs ascending a mountain peak. (35)
With their faces moist and dejected by tears, like lotus-pools with wet lotuses after the rain,
they lay down upon their respective places according to their rank, burning with grief as they watched her.
Surrounded on the palace roof by those women, that fair-limbed lady, emaciated by anxiety,
shone like a crescent moon in the midst of autumnal clouds encircled by streaks of lightning.
Among them, she who was distinguished by her speech, worthy of respect, and senior in age, embraced her from behind, wiped away her tears, and spoke these words: ||38||
O wife of a royal seer, grief is never appropriate for you while your husband remains devoted to dharma;
for in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, the forest hermitages are the desired inheritance. (39)
Generally, you know those women of the Śākya bulls who have gone forth for liberation;
for whom even their homes are like penance groves, having embraced the vow of virtuous wives as if it were a mere matter of desire.
If your husband has been carried away by another woman because of her superior beauty and virtues, then shed your tears!
For what woman of spirit, beauty, and noble qualities would not shed tears when her heart is wounded? (41)
Moreover, even if she were to encounter some misfortune, let there not be such tears as these;
for there is no grief whatsoever greater than that which befalls a woman of noble birth who regards her husband as a deity. (42)

But now, having played freely, being at ease and established in well-being, having seen no calamities, free from longing and having entered upon the Dharma—why do you weep in distress at a time for joy? (43)
Although she was addressed in this way by her in many ways out of affection, she did not regain her composure at all;
then another woman spoke to her with endearment, words that were pleasing to the mind and appropriate for the occasion. (44)
I speak the truth, for which I am firmly resolved: you shall soon behold your beloved once more.
Without you, that abode of beings will remain there like one deprived of consciousness. (45)
Even while Lakṣmī rests upon his lap, he would find no peace if you were not by his side;
yet, even when dire calamities have arrived, there would be no sorrow for him as long as he beholds you.
Go to your rest and restrain your tears; protect your eyes from shedding these hot tears.
That disposition of his toward you and that passion which he felt—because of separation from you, he will find no delight in the Dharma.
It might be argued here: "He will not cast off the saffron robe because of his noble birth and character.
But for one who has taken it up without true self-mastery and is now intent on returning home, what fault is there in letting it go again? (48)

Thus, being consoled by her young companions while her heart was stolen away by her lover, that beautiful woman fell to the ground before the Draviḍa, surrounded by her attendants like Rambhā in the presence of the Apsarases. 49.
The sixth canto, titled "The Lament of the Wife," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*, is completed.
The seventh canto: "The Lament of Nanda."
Then Nanda, wearing upon his body the insignia prescribed by the Teacher’s rule but not in his heart, was filled with shame by thoughts of his wife that occupied his mind; he did not rejoice.

Established in his pleasure garden, he did not attain tranquility due to the floral splendor of the month of spring, the all-encompassing assault of the flower-bannered god of love, and the very nature of youth which inclines one toward worldly enjoyment.

Standing dejectedly in the mango grove where bees were clustering and humming, he of the arms long as a yoke yawned deeply; having meditated upon his beloved, he drew her toward him as if drawing a bow.
Receiving from the mango trees a rain of delicate flowers like yellow powder,
he sighed deeply as he brooded upon his wife, like a newly captured elephant confined in a pen.

The remover of grief for those who seek refuge, yet the creator of sorrow for the arrogant, he took hold of the Ashoka tree and, overcome by grief, lamented for his beloved, whose groves were filled with lovely Ashoka blossoms. (5)
Beholding his beloved Priyaṅgu creeper— slender, dear to his beloved, and appearing as if terrified as she fled—
he, with tears in his eyes, remembered that tear-faced beloved who was as fair as the blossoms of the Priyaṅgu.
Seeing a cuckoo perched on the crest of a tilaka tree covered in blossoms,
he imagined it to be the white braid of his beloved as she leaned against the turret of her palace draped in white silken garments.
Seeing a blossoming *atimuktaka* creeper that had grown by embracing a mango tree at its side, he immediately fell into such reflection: "May that beautiful woman also embrace me. (8)

Even the *nāga* trees, though made formidable by their abundance of flowers, did not catch his eye there—resembling golden caskets filled with jewels yet appearing like trees in a wilderness to one who is suffering. (9)

Though they exhaled fragrance, those *gandhaparṇā* plants, full of scent like celestial courtesans (*gandharvaveśyā*), did not captivate the nose of him whose mind was elsewhere and whose soul was filled with grief; rather, they pierced his heart.

The forest, resounding with cuckoos with throats reddened by passion and blue-throated peacocks, as well as with joyful and delighted mynas and bees repeatedly licking at honey, captivated his mind. (11)

There, burning within his heart with the fire of passion— whose fuel was his wife, whose smoke was discursive thought, and whose crest was darkness— he abandoned his fortitude and lamented various things.
Today I understand that what they have done, will do, and are doing is exceedingly difficult:
those who, having abandoned their beloved with tearful faces, have practiced, will practice, and are indeed practicing asceticism. (13)
In this world, there is no bond as firm as this: neither one made of wood, nor of fiber, nor of iron;
rather, it is this very face, so mobile in its eyes and so charming in its speech. (14)

For those snares made of affection can be traversed by cutting and breaking them through one's own manliness and the strength of friends; yet, without knowledge and austerity, it is impossible to be liberated from the snare consisting of attachment. (15)
That knowledge which leads to peace does not exist in me, nor is there any harshness in me, for I am compassionate by nature;
yet I am possessed by desire and the Buddha is my teacher, and I remain as one situated within the turning of the wheel.

For even though I have assumed the marks of a monk and am instructed by my brother, the seer, who is my superior, I find no peace in any circumstance, like a cakravāka bird separated from its beloved. (17)
Even now, that remains in my heart: when the mirror was disturbed by me, she, feigning anger, spoke to me while laughing mockingly, "O rogue, how have you become so? (18)
The words she spoke to me with tearful eyes and a face of trembling gaze—"O you whose body is so exceptionally fair"—still weigh upon my heart even today. (19)
Having understood the true seat, this mendicant, dwelling by a mountain waterfall, meditates with composure;
surely he is not attached to anything as I am, for he sits thus, peaceful and as if satisfied. (20)
Disregarding the song of the male cuckoos and casting no eye upon the splendor of spring, this disciplined youth studies his scriptures; I suspect that his heart is drawn away by his beloved.
Homage be to him whose resolve is firm, whose curiosity and wonder have ceased;
to him who is peaceful in soul, whose pride has subsided within, who wanders about free from longing. (22)

Who could possess fortitude while gazing upon the water with its lotuses and the blossoming forest frequented by cuckoos, during the month of Madhu, which acts as the adversary to righteousness, especially for one in the bloom of youth? (23)
By their demeanor, pride, gait, grace, smiles, anger, intoxication, and speech, women captivated the hosts of gods, kings, and sages; why then would they not captivate someone like me? (24)

For even Hiraṇyaretas, overcome by desire, consorted with Svāhā; and Madhava, lacking in that same strength and creative power, consorted with Ahalyā. Being thus conquered by women, what indeed can be said of me, a mere mortal? (25)
We have heard that Sūrya, having conceived passion for Saraṇyū, fashioned [an image] for her pleasure;
for, having united with the mare in the form of a horse, he begot those two Aśvins. (26)

For the sake of a woman, a battle took place for many years between Vaivasvata and Agni, whose intellects were obsessed with enmity and whose self-control and fortitude had faltered; who else here would not be moved by the cause of a woman? (27)
Out of desire, that most excellent sage Vasiṣṭha sent his rosary to a dog-cooker woman;
from her was born his son Kapiñjalāda, who, like Viśvāmitra, consumed the earth and its waters.
The sage Parāśara, whose arrow was his curse, consorted with Kālī, who was born from the womb of a fish;
from her, his high-souled son Dvaipāyana was begotten, the divider of the Vedas. (29)

And Dvaipāyana, though devoted to righteousness, took his pleasure with a courtesan’s wife among the Kāśis—she by whom he was struck with her foot, adorned with jingling anklets, like a cloud by a flash of lightning. (30)
Likewise, Aṅgiras, the son of Brahmā, whose mind was overcome by passion, resorted to Sarasvatī;
there his son Sārasvata was born, who became the restorer of the lost Veda. (31)
Likewise, at the sacrifice of the royal sage Dilīpa, Kaśyapa stood waiting for a celestial woman;
taking up the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), he cast his own flowing vital energy (*ātma-tejas*) into the fire, from which Aśita was born. (32)
Likewise, Aṅgada, having reached the culmination of asceticism, was overcome by desire and went to Yamunā;
there he begot Sāraṅgajuṣṭa upon Rathītara, who was most wise. (33)

Having beheld the princess Śāntā, even though he was dwelling in a forest that was itself tranquil, the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga wavered from his fortitude, like a mountain with lofty peaks during an earthquake. (34)
He who, indifferent to sense-objects, abandoned his kingdom to attain the state of a Brahman-sage and took refuge in the forest—
Gādhi’s son, though carried away by Ghṛtācī, perceived that eleven years were but a single day.
In the same way, Sthūlaśiras, touched by the arrows of Kandarpa, fainted for Rambhā;
he who, out of lust and anger, was indifferent to all else, cursed her when she refused him.
And when his beloved Pramadvarā had her life-force snatched away by a serpent, Ruru killed snakes again and again; yet he did not do so out of anger, but rather to protect his ascetic merit.

The grandson of the Moon, marked with the qualities of fame, the son of Budha, possessing the power of a god—having thus meditated upon the Apsaras Urvaśī, the royal sage Aiḍa fell into a state of madness. (38)
Passionate for Menakā on the mountain peak, that Tālajaṅgha, being possessed by lust, was struck angrily with his foot by Viśvāvasu like a hintāla tree struck by a thunderbolt. (39)
When the supreme woman had met her destruction in the waters of the Gaṅgā, King Janhu, his mind overwhelmed by the god of love,
held back the Gaṅgā with his two arms like Maināka, the lord of mountains.

And King Śantanu, the lamp of his lineage and son of Pratīpa, though possessed of a glorious body, reeled from the separation from the Gaṅgā like a *sāla* tree whose roots have been washed away by the waters of the Gaṅgā; he was no longer master of himself.

Lamenting that woman Urvaśī— who had been carried off by Saunandakin as if she were the earth herself— Somavarman, whose armor was his virtuous conduct, wandered about with his very heart pierced by the arrow of love.
When his wife died, King Bhīmaka, who possessed formidable power upon the earth, followed her in death;
he was renowned as Senāka by virtue of his strength, a commander of armies like a god who had taken up his host.
When her husband Śantanu had gone to heaven, Janamejaya, desiring to seize Kālī, encountered his death at the hands of Bhīṣma; yet he did not abandon the passion directed toward her.
Pāṇḍu had certainly been cursed by Madana, saying, "You shall meet your death in the company of a woman";
therefore, though he was one who avoided what is unfit to be pursued, he did not reflect upon death and went to Mādrī due to the curse of the great seer.
Even such multitudes of gods, kings, and sages have fallen under the sway of women through the power of desire;
being weak in both wisdom and essential strength, how much more so am I, overwhelmed by grief at not seeing my beloved? (46)

Therefore, I shall go back home once more and fulfill my desire according to the prescribed rites; for the outward mark [of a religious life] is not fitting for one whose mind is on other things, whose senses are unsteady, and who has fallen from the path of Dharma. (47)

Holding an alms-bowl in his hand, having shaved his head, having cast aside pride, and having donned a discolored garment—he for whom there is neither elation nor steadfastness, and no peace—exists and yet does not exist, like a painted lamp. (48)
He who has renounced the world yet has not renounced sensual passion, who wears the saffron robe yet is not free from impurity;
who carries an alms-bowl yet is not a worthy vessel for virtues—he, though bearing the outward signs, is neither a householder nor a mendicant. (49)

"Even my reflection that it is not right to abandon the mark once one has accepted it as possessing a logical connection—that too vanishes when I consider how those other heroic kings, having left the forest hermitages, returned to their homes. (50)

For Śālva’s lord, along with his son, as well as Ambarīṣa, Rāma, Andha, and Antideva the Sāṃskṛti—having cast off their bark garments, they again donned fine silken cloths; and having cut off their matted locks, they wore crowns once more. (51)
Therefore, before my preceptor goes from here for the sake of alms, I shall depart from this place for home, casting off my saffron robes;
for it is a source of affliction for one of faltering mind and clouded intellect to bear the venerable emblem [of asceticism].
Neither would there be any purpose for the next world, nor would this world of living beings exist for one whose intellect is impaired. ||52||

What is this face, clouded with tears, that reveals the darkness dwelling within your heart? Take courage and restrain this agitation; for neither weeping nor tranquility is becoming here.
Feeling arises invariably in two ways: in the mind and in the body alone;
likewise, there are only two kinds of physicians for these two, those who are skilled in the application of learning and ritual injunctions. (3)
Therefore, if you have any bodily ailment, let it be told quickly and fully to the physician;
for one who conceals his illness soon meets with severe misfortune. (4)
Now, tell me of this mental suffering; I shall declare the remedy for it.
For those who know the inner self and are discerning examiners are the physicians for a mind possessed by passion and ignorance. (5)
"O gentle one, tell me the whole truth, if you think it should be told to me;
for the ways of minds are manifold, and great families possess many secrets. (6)
Thus urged by him, desiring then to declare his own resolve,
he took the other by the hand with his own hand and entered another part of the forest.
Then they both sat down there in that pure vine-cottage, which was exhaling the fragrance of flowers;
they were as if embraced by the tender sprouts, which were moved by gentle breezes. (8)

Then he spoke of his intended course of action—words held within by heavy sighs—which, though difficult for a learned man who has renounced the world to utter, were addressed to the mendicant whose speech was refined by learning. (9)

If it were consistent with your constant practice of dharma and your mind of loving-kindness toward all living beings, then this desire for my welfare would befit you, who are compassionate by nature and virtuous. (10)

For this very reason, I have a particular desire to speak with you, who are a speaker of what is fitting; for I would not reveal this state of mind even to an unvirtuous person, were he to speak to me, if he were of a fickle nature.
Listen to this from me in brief: I find no delight in the practice of dharma without my beloved, like a kinnara of restrained seed wandering upon mountain peaks without his mate. (12)
Averse to the happiness of dwelling in the forest, my desire is to go home;
for without her, I find no peace, like a king deprived of supreme sovereignty.
