Alas, how pitiable! This fickle deer, longing for his herd and having escaped from the great fear of the hunter, now seeks to enter the snare, deceived by the sound of singing. (15)

Indeed, a bird caught in a net was liberated by a person seeking his welfare; now, wandering through the forest abounding in fruits and flowers, he desires to enter his own cage of his own accord. (16)

The young elephant, indeed, having been pulled out by his mother from the uneven riverbed thick with mud, now wishes to cross that same crocodile-infested stream once more, driven by the thirst for water. ||17||
Sleeping in a shelter infested with snakes, a youth who was awakened by another who had woken up, being truly deluded, desired to seize the fierce serpent himself. (18)
Having flown up from a forest tree set ablaze by a great fire, the bird, free from distress, desires once more to alight there out of longing for its nest. (19)
Helpless indeed through the swoon of passion, separated from his beloved due to the fear of a hawk, the jīvajīvaka bird finds neither fortitude nor shame; he lives piteously. (20)
Lacking self-discipline, possessed by thirst, and devoid of both compassion and wisdom, the wretched dog indeed desires to eat again its own vomit. (21)
Thus, having meditated upon him who was tormented by the grief of love and having gazed at him repeatedly, that ascetic, desiring his welfare, spoke these virtuous yet unpleasant words: (22)

If you do not investigate what is auspicious and inauspicious, but have your mind fixed solely upon sense objects, and if you have attained birth without having gained the eye of wisdom, then you shall find no delight in the highest good. (23)

For one whose mind is not detached and whose self is unsteady, no delight in the Dharma is ordained—whether in hearing, grasping, or retaining it, nor in the realization of the ultimate truth or the tranquility of the mind. (24)

But for one who perceives the defects in sense-objects, who is contented, pure, and free from pride, whose mind is disciplined in the practices of tranquility—for such a person of perfected intellect, there is no delight in worldly pleasures. (25)
The thirsty man delights in the glory of wealth; the fool delights in the pleasure of sensual desire;
but the virtuous person, having transcended enjoyments through knowledge, delights in tranquility. 26.

Moreover, the mind of one who is renowned, wise, of noble birth, and a wearer of honored signs, does not incline toward domestic life, just as a mountain does not bend under the force of the wind. (27)

He who, disregarding his own independent self-mastery, should long for dependence on another, would be like one established on the auspicious path of tranquility who longs for a house full of faults. 28.

Just as one who has escaped from captivity might, when struck by calamity, enter bondage once again, so too might one who has gone to the forest seek out the bondage known as the household once more. (29)

And that man who, having abandoned strife, should desire to serve strife once again—he, a fool with uncontrolled senses, would abandon his own wife and seek out one who is herself the very embodiment of strife. (30)
Like poisonous creepers that have taken root, like caves infested with serpents that have been disturbed, or like drawn swords that have been grasped—women indeed end in calamity. (31)
Women who are intoxicated bring about intoxication; women who are free from intoxication bring about fear.
Since they thus bring about both faults and fear, how indeed can they be worthy of cultivation? 32.

Since even one's own kin is divided by kin, and even a friend by those who are friends, it is unrefined women—who are treacherous and skilled at observing the faults of others—who conduct themselves in such a manner. (33)
That noble-born men become wretched, that they commit every kind of improper rashness, and that they impetuously charge into the front of the army—of all this, women are the cause. (34)
They captivate with their lovely speech, yet they strike with a sharpened mind;
honey resides in the words of women, but in their hearts lies the great poison Hālāhala. (35)
Even a fire that burns can be grasped; even the bodiless wind can be grasped;
even an enraged serpent can be grasped—but the mind of women cannot be grasped. (36)
They do not consider physical beauty, nor fortune, nor intellect, nor lineage, nor prowess;
women strike out without distinction, like rivers teeming with shoals of crocodiles. (37)

A woman does not remember sweet words, nor endearments, nor any affection; once she has been won, she is as fickle as a lightning flash, and thus she is not to be relied upon here, just like enemies. (38)
When men do not give, women become playful; when they give, they fall into confusion.
Toward those who bow before them, they become arrogant, yet they are most satisfied with those who are proud. (39)
They behave like masters toward those possessed of virtues, and like sons toward those devoid of virtues;
they behave with greed toward the wealthy, and with contempt toward those who lack wealth. (40)

Just as a cow, even when led away, continues to graze by moving from one pasture to another, so too does a woman, having gone elsewhere, take her pleasure there, disregarding her former affection. 41.
For women may indeed enter the funeral pyre and even follow [their husbands] at the cost of their own lives;
they may even endure restraints, yet they do not carry affection with their true inner being. 42.
Those women who, in some rare instances, somehow delight their husbands by regarding them as deities, delight only their own hearts a thousandfold through their own fickle-mindedness. (43)
It is said that Senajit’s daughter desired a dog-cooker (outcaste), while Kumudvatī desired the enemy of fish (the moon);
likewise, Bṛhadrathā desired the king of beasts (a lion). Thus, there is no limit to the conduct of women. 44.

The descendants of Kuru, Haihaya, and Vṛṣṇi, as well as Śambara—who possessed armor made of many illusions—and the sage Gautama of fierce austerities, all fell under the sway of passion stirred by women. (45)
Ungrateful, ignoble, and fickle—such is the mind of women;
how could a wise man allow his heart to be attached to them, who are so unstable in nature? (46)
If you do not perceive that their hearts are subtle, dualistic, and inauspicious, why do you not see that the bodies of women—a leaking, impure house of unreality—are likewise so? (47)
Day after day, you adorn yourself with grooming, garments, and ornaments;
yet, with your vision shrouded by darkness, you perceive this as auspicious and fail to realize its impurity. (48)
Or perhaps you perceive that body as impure, yet you possess no true knowledge [of its nature];
for you perform a fragrant ritual action for the sake of pacifying the impurity from which it originates. (49)
If ointments, collyrium, garlands, jewels, pearls, gold, and fine silks are considered excellent, then what is innate to women? Let that purity be sought among them. (50)

If that beautiful woman of yours were to become covered in the mire of dirt, naked, with her nails, teeth, and body hair left in their natural state, she would certainly no longer be beautiful to you today. (51)
What compassionate person would touch a woman who flows with impurity, like a cracked vessel, were she not covered by a mere skin as thin as a fly's wing? (52)

If you perceive the bodies of women as nothing more than a cage of bones wrapped in skin, and yet you are forcibly drawn by passion—then you are truly merciless, for lust is indeed devoid of self-control. (53)
Imagining beauty in what is impure—among nails, teeth, skin, hair, and body hair—O lack of discernment, do you not see both the true nature and the origin of women? (54)
Having understood that both mind and body are particularly full of faults, let the fickle mind, which yearns for worldly existence, be restrained by the power of analytical reflection. (55)
Learned, wise, and of noble birth, you are a vessel for the highest tranquility;
having approached it, you ought not, by any means, to break the vow again. (56)
For one of noble birth, high-minded, fond of fame, and desiring great respect, even death is better for one of steady soul than life for one who has fallen from discipline. (57)
For just as one who has donned armor and taken up his bow becomes censurable if he flees from the battlefield while standing in his chariot,
so too is one who has accepted the mendicant's mark and entered upon the life of a beggar.
Likewise, one whose horse-like senses have been carried away by desire becomes an object of reproach. ||58||
Just as one who, adorned with supreme ornaments, garments, and garlands, wanders for alms while bearing a bow and a shimmering variegated crown, is an object of laughter;
so too is one who, having accepted deformity and subsisting on the food of others, yet remains full of craving and intent upon the pleasures of the household—a sight fit for laughter. (59)
Just as a boar, having eaten fine food and even lying upon a most excellent bed, would run back toward its familiar filth once it has emerged from it;
so too, one who hears what is beneficial and has tasted the virtuous bliss of tranquility [might still run back to the world].
Thirsting for sensual pleasures, one might abandon the peaceful forest and long for the home.
Just as a torch held in the hand burns when its flame is fanned by the wind, just as a serpent, impelled by rage, bites when stepped upon by the foot,
and just as even a tiger cub kills when seized within the house, so too does association with women lead to manifold misfortunes.
Having understood these defects inherent in women that are fixed within the mind and body,
and considering sensual pleasure to be as unstable as river water, leading only to affliction and sorrow;
and seeing the world to be as fragile as an unbaked clay vessel, assailed by death—
Form an incomparable resolve for liberation; you ought not to feel such longing [for worldly things]. ||62||
The eighth canto, titled "The Obstacle of Women," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The ninth canto: "Censure of Pride."
Even though he was thus addressed by that monk, he did not attain tranquility regarding his beloved;
for, thinking only of her at that time, he did not hear his words, as if deprived of consciousness.
Just as a dying patient does not accept the beneficial words of a physician who desires his welfare,
even so he, intoxicated by his strength, beauty, and youth, did not accept those beneficial words of his.
And it is not surprising if the mind of one whose self is shrouded in darkness should be overcome by the evil of passion;
for the evil of a man departs only when that darkness has reached its end and become diminished.
Then, observing him thus cast down by his strength, beauty, and youth,
and seeing that he was resolved upon departing for home, that ascetic instructed Nanda for the sake of his peace.
I understand strength, beauty, and fresh youth just as you understand them;
however, I perceive these three of yours as unstable, whereas you do not perceive them as such. (5)
For this body is a seat of disease, subject to old age, and as unstable as a tree on a riverbank;
it is as fragile as water-foam, yet you do not realize this, for which reason you imagine yourself to be established in strength.

When the body is seen to be on the verge of ruin through either the non-observance or the excessive observance of the activities of food, drink, seating, and transport, for what reason do you maintain pride in your strength? (7)

When the world is afflicted by misfortunes such as cold, heat, disease, old age, hunger, and the like—wasting away like water in the hot month under the rays of the sun—how can you, proud of your strength, think otherwise? (8)

When this body, consisting of skin, bone, flesh, and blood, subsists by means of food, it is perpetually afflicted and requires constant remedial action; how can you be deluded, thinking "I am endowed with strength"? (9)

Just as a man might desire to cross a turbulent great ocean by relying on an unbaked earthen jar, so too does one who exerts effort for the sake of sense-objects exert strength while discarding a lofty but worthless elevation. (10)
In my view, this body is even more utterly devoid of substance than a jar made of clay;
for a jar, when maintained according to rule, may endure for a long time, whereas this physical frame breaks apart even when well-sustained. (11)

When the elements of water, earth, air, and fire—always mutually opposed like venomous serpents—are situated within the body and lead to misfortune, how can you, O bringer of disease, determine what strength there is? (12)
Serpents are pacified by mantras, but the humors (dhātus) cannot be subdued by mantras;
serpents bite only here and there, whereas the humors always afflict everything. (13)
For this body, though long tended with beds, seats, drinks, food, and virtues, does not tolerate even a single transgression, since it becomes enraged like a great venomous serpent. (14)
When one afflicted by cold resorts to fire, or one struck by the heat of summer longs for snow;
when one is possessed by hunger seeks food, or by thirst seeks water—whence comes strength, and what is it, how is it, and to whom does it belong? (15)
Thus, having understood that the body is afflicted by disease, you ought not to think, "I am possessed of strength.
The world is without essence, without end, and uncertain; in this impermanent world, strength is unstable. (16)

Where is that strength of the thousand-armed Arjuna Kārtavīrya, who was so proud of his power, whose arms were severed in battle by the descendant of Bhṛgu, just as a thunderbolt cleaves the great peaks of a mountain? (17)

Where is that strength of Hari, the drawer of Kaṃsa, who split the temples of the king of horses—that very Jarā who, with a single arrow, struck down him as old age strikes down supreme beauty in due course? (18)

Where was that strength of Namuci—the son of Diti, the harasser of the gods, the one with beautiful eyes—who stood in battle like the enraged God of Death himself, yet was slain by Indra with a mere fragment of foam? (19)

Where did that strength of the Kurus go when they were struck down in battle? Having blazed with speed and vigor like fires kindled by fuel at a sacrifice, they have now come to rest as ashes, their lives extinguished. (20)

Therefore, having understood that the strength of those who pride themselves on their power and vigor has been crushed, and reflecting upon how the world is subject to old age and death, you ought not to harbor conceit regarding strength. (21)
Whether you consider your strength to be great or not, engage first in battle with the senses;
for if you are victorious here, your strength is truly great, but if you are defeated, your strength is in vain.
For thus it is considered: those men who conquer enemies along with their horses, chariots, and elephants are not regarded as heroes;
rather, those wise ones who conquer the six flickering senses are considered the truest of heroes. (23)
And as for your thought, "I am handsome," O discerning one—let this also be considered:
where is that beauty, and where is that handsome body of Gada, Śāmba, and Sāraṇa? (24)

Just as a peacock, with its shimmering variegated eye-patterns, possesses a beautiful form by its very nature, so too, if you are truly possessed of beauty, you possess that form even without the quality of bodily adornment. (25)

O handsome one, tell me, what would he become if he were to choose the contrary—neither clothing nor water at the time of purification; or if he were not to apply the specific cleansing of the body? (26)
Observing that your youth has reached its prime, your mind is now turned toward the household for the sake of attaining sensual objects;
restrain it, for youth, like the current of a mountain river, flows swiftly and does not turn back. (27)
The season that has passed returns again; the moon, having waned, comes back once more.
But the water of rivers that has flowed away never returns, nor does the youth of men. 28.
When you see your face discolored, with wrinkled and distorted features, teeth decayed, eyebrows sagging, and luster lost—worn out and overcome by old age—then you will be free from pride. (29)
Having indulged for a long time in the finest intoxicating drink during the nights at the end of the day, a man becomes intoxicated;
yet no one, though intoxicated by strength, beauty, and youth, ever becomes so intoxicated as when one has not escaped old age. (30)

Just as sugarcane, when its juice has been completely squeezed out, lies upon the ground parched for the sake of fire, so too the body, crushed by the machine of old age and drained of its essence, remains only for death. (31)
Just as a saw, driven by two men, splits a towering piece of wood into many parts, so too does old age, joined with day and night, strike down these people who have grown tall. (32)

The thief of memory, the destroyer of the body, the ender of pleasure, the seizer of speech, hearing, and sight, the source of exhaustion, and the slayer of strength and vigor—for embodied beings, there is no enemy equal to old age. (33)
Knowing this—this great calamity of the world called old age, which is the guide to death—you ought not to ascend the ignoble pride of thinking, "I am handsome, strong, or young. (34)
For those whose minds are stained by passion, there is the notion of a body expressed as "I" and "mine"; abandon this grasping at it which exists in you during this Kali age.
If peace is to be attained, let go of it, for fear arises from the notions of "I" and "mine. (35)

When no one has mastery over this body as it is cast about by various afflictions, how can it be appropriate to consider this house known as the "body" as "I" or "mine," or as a dwelling for calamities? (36)

He who would always delight in a wretched house that is perpetually impure, yet constantly renovated and fragile—he, possessing perverted vision, would likewise delight in this body, which consists of foul elements, is impure, and is unstable and shifting. (37)

Just as a wicked king forcibly takes all taxes from his subjects and yet does not protect them, so too the body consumes all the means such as clothing and the like, and yet does not follow [the needs of] its owner. (38)

Just as grasses sprout from the earth without effort, whereas rice requires effort to grow, even so do sufferings arise without effort, while happiness arises through effort—or perhaps not at all. (39)

For one who drags about a distressed and flickering body, there is no happiness whatsoever in the ultimate sense; for what is called "happiness" is merely the pursuit of a remedy for suffering, and it is only when suffering has become slight that one perceives it as such. (40)

Just as even the slightest suffering that has arrived overcomes one regardless of the most desired happiness, so too, when suffering has arisen within oneself, no happiness whatsoever exists for anyone. 41.
If you do not understand that such a body is unstable and full of manifold suffering for the sake of its fruits,
then let the mind be restrained by the reins of fortitude from those flowing fruits, like a cow greedy for grain.
For sensual enjoyments do not lead to satisfaction, just as oblations do not satisfy a blazing fire.
In whatever measure one indulges in the pleasures of desire, to that same extent does longing for sense objects increase. (43)

Just as one afflicted by the calamity of leprosy finds no relief from the heat of its inflammation, so too one who has not conquered his senses, while pursuing the objects of the senses, attains no tranquility through the enjoyment of desires. 44.

For just as one might seek out diseases out of a desire for the pleasure of medicine, yet not seek them out when they have served their purpose, so too, though the body is a vessel of manifold suffering, one might delight in it through delusion out of a craving for sense objects. (45)
Indeed, by that very act, a person who desires what is harmful to another is considered that person's enemy;
for sense-objects, being the sole root of harm, must surely be abandoned like dangerous foes. (46)
Having been enemies intent on slaughter right here, they become friends to a person in the course of time;
yet desires are the cause of suffering both in this world and the next, and are never auspicious for anyone.
Just as the fruit of the *kimpāka* tree, though possessing flavor, color, and fragrance, leads to death when consumed and not to nourishment,
so too do sense objects lead to misfortune and not to well-being for one whose mind is fickle when they are indulged in.

Having understood this—this beneficial counsel, free from sin, endowed with the dharma of liberation and other virtues—accept my view, which is esteemed by the virtuous; or else, uttering your own words, declare your firm resolve. (49)

Thus addressed by that great ascetic with words that were both beneficial and abundant, Nanda found neither fortitude nor peace; like an elephant blinded by rut and excessive passion, his mind was clouded by intoxication. (50)

Then, having understood Nanda’s disposition— which was wavering, directed toward domestic pleasures rather than the Dharma— that monk, who examines the intentions, latent tendencies, and dispositions of sentient beings, [proceeded].
He spoke to the Buddha, the knower of reality.
The ninth canto, titled “A Reproach against Pride,” in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The tenth canto: “A Vision of Heaven.”
Then, having heard that Nanda was desirous of abandoning his noble vows, longing to see his wife, and wishing to enter his home—
devoid of joy and stripped of fortitude— the Sage, wishing to uplift him, called out to him.
Sucitta questioned him—who had attained the path of liberation yet had not yet reached its goal—regarding a lapse in his mind.
Bowed with shame before the modest one, he spoke his own conviction to that master of discernment.
Having perceived Nanda wandering in the darkness called "wife," the Sugata took him by the hand and leaped into the sky, like a virtuous man desiring to lift a stain out of water. (3)
Clad in saffron robes and radiant as gold, the two shone in the clear sky like a pair of cakravāka birds alighting upon a lake with their wings outspread and joined together.

They quickly arrived at the Himavat, which possesses the supreme fragrance of devadāru trees, abounds in rivers, lakes, and cascading springs, contains veins of gold ore, and is frequented by divine sages.
On that auspicious mountain, frequented by *cāraṇas* and *siddhas*, whose upper garment was formed by the smoke of sacrificial offerings,
those two stood like two islands in the sky which is otherwise inaccessible and without support.
While the Sage remained there with his senses stilled, Nanda gazed in wonder at the quarters of the sky,
and saw that the caves, the groves, and the forest-dwellers were both the ornament and the very protection of the mountain.
On that long, white peak, a peacock with its plumage gathered lay resting;
it shone like a beryl armlet upon the long, thick arm of Bala.
Resting upon a rock of the nature of a mind-disciplined sage, that lion shone with shoulders of yellow hue,
like the shattered silver armlet of Ambika, variegated with patterns of refined gold.

Moving with a playful gait, extended by fatigue, and keeping his tail to the left, the tiger shone like one descended from Mount Prasravaṇa, desiring to drink its waters and wishing to offer them to his ancestors. ||10||
On a tree with swaying kadamba blossoms on the slope of the Himalayas, a yak became entangled;
though he hung there, he was unable to sever his tail, just as a man of noble conduct cannot sever the affection born of his lineage.

And hosts of Kirātas, golden-hued, their bodies streaked with brilliant patterns like those of peacocks' tails, rushed forth from the caves like tigers springing out, resembling the volcanic eruptions of a mountain. (12)
In every direction, throngs of most beautiful Kinnarīs, wandering through the caves with enchanting hips, breasts, and bellies, shone like flowering creepers with blossoms for their hair. (13)
The monkeys roamed from mountain to mountain, seeking out devadāru trees;
yet they obtained no fruit from them and departed, like those who approach lords whose favors are in vain.

Then, seeing that female monkey being driven away from the herd—her face stained with crushed red lac and one of her eyes destroyed—the sage spoke these words to Nanda: 15. "Behold this female monkey, whose face is smeared with crushed red lac and whose sight is impaired; she is being driven away from that very troop."
"O Nanda, which do you consider more beautiful—this doe with her single failing eye, or that person for whom your affection has gone? (16)
Thus addressed by the Sugata, Nanda smiled slightly and said this:
"O Blessed One, where is that supreme woman, your bride, and where is this doe who causes distress to the mountain? (17)
Then the Sage, having heard his words and perceiving some underlying motive,
took Nanda by the hand and proceeded in that same manner to the pleasure-grove of King Vajradhara.
Where some trees assume their form in each season, while others assume it moment by moment, certain other trees bear the entire variegated splendor of all six seasons. (19)
Some cultivate fragrant and noble flowers, as well as various woven garlands and wreaths, and ear-ornaments that rival earrings in their beauty. (20)
Where red lotuses in full bloom make the trees appear like rows of lamps, while other trees, bearing blossoming blue lotuses, appear as if their eyes were wide open. (21)
Furthermore, there trees bear garments that are of various colors and white, illuminated by golden patterns; they are not woven from thread, being solid and single-pieces, yet exceedingly fine. (22)
Where trees bear such ornaments as necklaces, excellent jewels, supreme earrings, choice armlets, and anklets—ornaments worthy of heaven itself. (23)
And lotus ponds with unshaking bottoms grow lotuses with stalks of beryl and golden petals, with filaments of diamond sprouts—delightful to the touch and possessing the most excellent fragrance. (24)

There, trees variegated with jewels and gold—which serve as playmates for the inhabitants of the celestial abodes—bear as their fruit those various musical instruments, both long and broad, as well as hollow and solid ones. (25)

Where that Pārijāta tree stands like a king, shining with the qualities of its own majesty as it towers over the Mandāra trees, the Kuśeśaya lotuses, and the Kokanada trees bent down with blossoms. (26)

In that place, such trees—which provide the enjoyments of the denizens of heaven—were always produced upon the surface of the field of Triviṣṭapa, ploughed by the tireless plows of austerity and virtuous conduct. (27)
There, birds appeared with faces like realgar, eyes resembling crystal,
wings that were pale with crimson-tipped edges, and legs that were madder-colored with white halves.
Furthermore, other birds known as śiñjirikas roam about, adorned with variegated golden plumage and clear, sapphire-blue eyes, captivating the mind and ear with their songs.
Where birds roam, adorned by creepers that are crimson at their tips, golden-yellow in their middles,
and the color of lapis lazuli at their bases.
Others, winged creatures named Rociṣṇus, possessing the color of blazing fire with mouths as if aflame,
wander about casting glances with their bodies while captivating the Apsarases with their auspicious sounds.

There, those who have performed meritorious deeds—whether low, superior, or middling by their own actions—dwell in self-effulgence, sporting with whatever they desire, ever joyful, free from affliction, free from decay, and free from sorrow. (32)
There, the Apsarases, sporting wantonly, captivate the weary minds of those rich in asceticism who had previously resolved to purchase heaven by means of the price paid through their penance.

Beholding that world in perpetual festival, free from weariness, sleep, passion, sorrow, and disease, Nanda considered this world of men— subject to old age and death and always afflicted— to be like a cemetery.
And Nanda beheld that grove of Indra on all sides, his eyes wide with wonder;
and the Apsarases, filled with joy, surrounded him while looking at one another with pride.

Always youthful, with love as their sole pursuit, and common to all who have performed meritorious deeds, these divine women—possessing faultless bodies—are the resort of the gods and the very foundation of the fruit of asceticism. (36)

Some sang with deep and lofty voices; others plucked lotuses with grace; and still others danced out of mutual joy, performing various graceful movements while their necklaces were broken by the pressure of their breasts.
The faces of some among them shone with their swaying earrings within the forest, like lotuses shaken by *kāraṇḍava* ducks emerging from mines where the leaves have been swept away. (38)
Seeing them emerge from the depths of the forest like streaks of lightning from rain-clouds, Nanda’s body trembled with passion, like the reflection of the moon in rippling water. (39)
Then, by means of his mind, he captivated their divine form and graceful gestures;
with eyes drawn by curiosity, he felt passion as if from a longing for union. (40)
His thirst having been aroused and longing for the Apsarases, he was overcome by the distress of his agitation in the pursuit of them;
dragged away by the chariot of his mind, whose horse was his restless senses, he found no steadfastness.
Just as a person makes a soiled garment even dirtier with alkaline salt—not for the sake of removing the stain, but for the sake of producing more dirt—so did the sage draw passion toward him. (42)
Just as a physician, desiring to extract humors from the body, might further exert himself to cause distress,
so the Sage, wishing to destroy his passion, brought about an even greater surge of passion.
Just as the radiance of the thousand-rayed sun rising in the darkness destroys the light of a lamp, so too does the splendor of the apsarases eclipse the brilliance of women in the world of men. 44.
A great form destroys a minute form, and a loud sound destroys a faint sound;
a severe illness destroys a mild illness—every great cause leads to the destruction of the small. (45)
And by the power of the Sage, Nanda was able to endure that sight which others could not bear;
for the splendor of the celestial nymphs' bodies would have burned the mind of one who is weak and has not yet transcended passion. (46)
Then, perceiving that Nanda’s passion had been aroused and that his own passion for his wife had ceased, the dispassionate Sage, desiring to counteract passion with passion, spoke these words. (47)
"O inhabitant of heaven, look at these women and speak the truth as it is:
how are they regarded by you in terms of beauty and virtue, or what is that person after whom your mind has gone? (48)

Then Nanda, his gaze fixed solely upon the apsarases and his inner heart set ablaze by the fire of passion, spoke these words with joined palms, his mind attached to desire and his voice faltering: (49)
O Lord, in that interval during which this bay mare has her gaze stolen away by your bride,
in that very interval your poor bride will perceive you as a corporeal *apsaras*.
Just as I previously had no regard for any other women upon seeing my wife,
so now I have no regard at all for her upon seeing their beauty.
Just as someone who has been scorched by a mild heat might be burned by a great fire, so too, having first been tormented by mild passion, I am now being consumed by this fire of passion. (52)

Therefore, sprinkle me with the water of your words before I am consumed by that fire of passion which, like the enemy of the lotus, now desires to burn me—just as a rising fire consumes dry grass along with the tops of trees. (53)
Be gracious; I am sinking, O Sage—release me! You possess the fortitude of the earth, yet I have no fortitude left.
I shall give up my life, O you whose mind is liberated; grant the nectar of your words to one who is about to die.

For I have been bitten in the heart by the serpent of passion, which possesses useless enjoyments as its body, the view of frustration as its eyes, negligence as its fangs, and the fire of the poison of darkness; therefore, O Great Physician, provide me with the antidote. (55)
No one bitten by this serpent of passion remained established in their own self;
indeed, even the mind of Śantanu—the wise one whose body was slender and whose soul was as immovable as a mountain—became deluded between wakefulness and sleep.
Since you, the distinguished refuge, are present, I take shelter with you so that, while dwelling here, I may not wander from direction to direction;
and so that, having attained the end of my calamities, I may reach my final rest—do this for me as I speak thus, being a virtuous man. (57)

Then Gautama, the moon among great sages who dispels the darkness of the world and has abandoned all darkness, spoke to him as he sought to strike his heart—like the moon that dispels the darkness which has arisen at night. (58)
Embracing fortitude, shaking off agitation, and restraining both your learning and your mind, listen:
if you desire these women, then perform here the highest austerity for the sake of attaining the pure goal. (59)
For these cannot be won by force, nor by service, nor by gifts, nor by beauty; indeed, they are carried away by the practice of Dharma. If you have joy, then practice the Dharma with devotion. (60)

Dwelling here in heaven together with the gods, amidst delightful forests and ageless women—this is the fruit of one's own auspicious karma; it was not given by another, nor did it arise without a cause. (61)
On earth, a man may or may not at some time obtain women through such labors as archery and the like;
however, it is beyond doubt that through the practice of dharma in this world, those of meritorious deeds shall become [their companions] in heaven.
Therefore, being vigilant and intent upon your religious observance, take delight therein if you desire the celestial nymphs;
and I shall be your guarantor in this matter regarding your firm vow, so that you will certainly attain them.
From that point on, established in the thought that this was supreme, he exercised the highest fortitude toward the Great Sage;
then the sage, descending like the wind from the sky, took hold of him and returned once more to the surface of the earth.
The tenth canto, titled "The Vision of Heaven," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is complete.
The eleventh canto: The Inferiority of Heaven.
Then, seeing those women wandering in the Nandana grove,
Nanda bound his restless and difficult-to-tame mind to the pillar of self-restraint.
Having fixed the celestial nymphs in his heart, he—whose taste for the renunciation of worldly life had waned and who resembled a fading lotus—practiced the Dharma devoid of flavor. ||2||

Likewise, having been one whose senses were restless and whose range of sensory objects was dear to him, he became one of restrained senses solely through mastery over the objects of the senses. ||3||
Skilled in the ways of sensual pleasure yet faltering in the conduct of a monk,
he practiced the holy life, firmly supported by his supreme teacher.
Through the restraint and tranquility [of his mind] and through the intensity of his passion, he was both cooled and dried up by their union, like water and fire. ||5||
Although he was naturally handsome, he attained an extreme state of disfigurement through his longing for the celestial nymphs and by his prolonged practice of ascetic discipline.
Even during conversations concerning his wife, he who was nonetheless fond of his wife remained as if free from passion; he neither rejoiced nor was he agitated.
Knowing him to be thus resolved and turned away from passion for his wife, Ānanda approached Nanda and spoke these words out of affection: (8)
Ah! How well-suited is this undertaking to his learning and his noble lineage—if he remains established in self-restraint, healthy in mind, and steadfast in his discipline. (9)
Since this consciousness has arisen in one who is deeply attached to desires, full of passion, and whose soul is intent upon sense-objects, it could not have been produced by a minor cause. (10)
A mild disease is averted with little effort;
a powerful one perishes—or perhaps does not—only through powerful efforts. ||11||
The mental affliction that arose within you was powerful and difficult to overcome;
yet, since it has been turned back, you are in every way possessed of fortitude. (12)

It is difficult for one who is ignoble to achieve goodness, and for one who is proud to achieve gentleness; it is difficult for a greedy person to practice renunciation, and for one who is passionate to maintain celibacy. (13)
I have, however, one doubt regarding this observance and your steadfastness;
I wish for your reassurance on this matter, if you think it should be spoken. (14)
A statement spoken with sincerity should not be understood otherwise; for a virtuous person does not perceive even harsh words as harsh when the underlying intention is pure. (15)
For that which is beneficial is unpleasant, and that which is pleasant is not beneficial;
but that which is both pleasant and beneficial is as rare as medicine that is both delicious and wholesome. (16)
Trust, acting for one's benefit, sharing in both joy and sorrow, forbearance, and affection—this is the conduct of friendship among the virtuous. (17)
This which I wish to say to you is out of affection, not from a desire to harm;
for my intention is to speak of what is for your own welfare, since I cannot remain indifferent.
"You are said to practice the Dharma as a hireling for the Apsarases;
is this a reality, or is it such a joke? (19)
If, first of all, I were to speak here of what is true—that is, the medicine for this [disease]—then I would be expressing the very passion (rajas) of those who speak with arrogance. (20)
Then, having been struck in the heart by him with gentle words,
he reflected for a long time, sighed deeply, and sat with his face slightly cast downwards.
Then, having understood his gesture which indicated the intention of his mind,
Ānanda spoke words that were unpleasant yet sweet in their ultimate consequence.
From your appearance, I perceive your purpose regarding the Dharma;
having understood it, both laughter and compassion have arisen within me toward you. (23)
Just as someone might carry a heavy stone on their shoulder for the sake of a seat, so too are you prepared to bear the burden of religious observances for the sake of sensual pleasures. (24)
Just as a proud ram butts another with the desire to strike,
so too is this celibacy of yours for the sake of [further] non-celibacy.
Just as merchants desire to sell their merchandise out of a longing for profit, so too is your practice of dharma like a commodity; it does not lead to peace.
Just as a farmer sows seed for the sake of a specific fruit, so too have you abandoned sense objects out of a longing for those very objects. (27)
Just as one might desire a disease out of a wish for the pleasure of its remedy, so do you seek suffering through thirst for sense objects. (28)
Just as one who sees honey does not look toward the precipice, so do you see the celestial nymphs and fail to perceive your fall at the end. (29)
With the fire of desire blazing in your heart while your body maintains its vow, what kind of celibacy is this for you, who are not a celibate in mind? (30)
Since you have existed in saṃsāra, hundreds of apsarases have been obtained and abandoned by you; why, then, do you still feel desire for them? (31)

Fire is not satisfied by fuel, nor is the salt-water ocean by water; likewise, one who possesses thirst is not satisfied by sensual pleasures. Therefore, sensual pleasures do not lead to satisfaction.

If there is no satisfaction, how can there be peace? And if there is no peace, how can there be happiness? If there is no happiness, how can there be joy? And if there is no joy, how can there be delight? (33)
If you desire to sport, then let your mind be fixed upon the inner self;
for there is no pleasure equal to that of the inner self, which is both tranquil and blameless. (34)
There is no need for musical instruments there, nor for women, nor for ornaments;
you shall enjoy yourself with that delight alone, wherever you may be situated. (35)
Mental suffering remains powerful as long as craving persists;
therefore, cut off that craving, for suffering exists only where there is craving or its absence. (36)
Whether in prosperity or in adversity, by day or by night, peace does not arise for one who is possessed of craving for sensual pleasures. (37)
The longing for sensual pleasures is painful, and there is no satisfaction even when they are attained;
separation from them inevitably brings grief, and such separation is certain even in heaven. (38)
Even after performing difficult deeds and attaining that which is hard to find in heaven, he returns once more to the world of men, just as one returns to one's own home from abroad. (39)
When no wholesome merit remains for one who has fallen away, he is reborn among the animals, in the world of the ancestors, or in hell. (40)
For him who has enjoyed even the most excellent objects of sense in heaven, but has now fallen and is afflicted by suffering—what pleasure can that [past enjoyment] provide? (41)
Out of compassion for living beings, Śibi gave even his own flesh to a hawk;
yet, despite performing such a difficult deed, he fell from heaven. (42)
He who was formerly a king went to share half the throne of Śakra;
having attained the state of a god in due time, Māndhātṛ fell back down again. (43)
Even after ruling over the gods, Nahuṣa fell to the earth;
having reportedly attained the state of a serpent, he is not released from it even today. 44.
In the same way, King Elivila, though refined by royal conduct, went to heaven but fell from there again and, it is said, became a tortoise in the ocean. (45)
Bhūridyumna, Yayāti, and those other bulls among kings,
having purchased heaven through their deeds, abandoned it once again upon its exhaustion.
The Asuras, who were formerly gods but whose splendor had been snatched away by the Suras, went to Pātāla for refuge, grieving for that lost glory. (47)
Furthermore, even for the royal sages, or for the asuras, or for the gods and others, hundreds of great Indras have fallen; thus, even greatness is not stable. (48)
Having graced the assembly of Indra, Upendra, possessing the prowess of Indra,
fell to the earth from the midst of the Apsarases, his karma exhausted, while emitting a sound.
"Alas, Caitraratha! Alas, the pond! Alas, Mandākinī! Alas, my beloved!"—thus the inhabitants of heaven, wailing in distress, fall to the earth. (50)
For even those wishing to die experience intense suffering here in this world;
how much more so for those who, having enjoyed happiness, fall from heaven at the end? (51)
Dust clings to their garments, the finest garlands wither, sweat breaks out upon their limbs, and they find no pleasure in their seats. (52)
These are the first signs of the falling away from heaven of the celestial dwellers,
just as undesirable omens are for mortals who are about to die.
Whatever happiness arises for those who enjoy desires in heaven, and whatever suffering there is for those falling [from it], suffering alone is distinguished as superior. (54)
Therefore, having realized that heaven is undesirable, provides no protection, is untrustworthy, fails to satisfy, and is subject to decay, set your mind upon liberation (apavarga). ||55||
For although the sage Udraka reached the bodiless peak of existence (bhavāgra),
at the end of his karma he fell from there and will enter an animal womb.
By means of seven years of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), Sunetra went from here to the Brahma-world;
yet he returned once more and entered the dwelling of a womb.
And when even those dwelling in heaven, though possessing sovereign power, are subject to decay, what wise person indeed would long for a residence in heaven that is destined to perish? (58)
Just as a bird bound by a string returns again and again even though it has flown far away, so too the world, bound by the string of ignorance, returns once more even though it has gone far. (59)
Just as one who has paid off his debt and been released from bondage by a guarantor might enjoy the pleasures of his home and, having fulfilled the term, enter into bondage again;
even so, he reached heaven through self-restraints such as meditation, which acted like a guarantor.
When those activities have been performed in due time and the objects of enjoyment have been consumed, he draws the earth back again.
Just as fish in a pond, their minds heedless because they have entered the inner net,

move about freely in the water unaware of the calamity born of confinement; so too do those who dwell in heaven, absorbed in meditation, remain unaware of their misfortune while they believe their purpose has been fulfilled within the inner worlds.
They consider Śiva, the infallible and eternal, to be their own abode, which brings them back [to rebirth]. ||61||
Perceiving this world to be enveloped by birth, disease, death, and calamity, wandering through cyclic existence among gods, humans, hell-beings, animals, and ancestors—
[seek] that which is a refuge, fearless, auspicious, immortal, undecaying, free from sorrow, and the deathless nectar.
For that reason, practice the holy life (brahmacarya) and abandon your wavering desire for heaven.
The eleventh canto, titled "The Inferiority of Heaven," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*, is completed.
The Twelfth Canto:
Thus exhorted— "You practice Dharma with the aid of the Apsaras Vivekā"— then...
Then Nanda was overcome with great shame because of Ānanda. ||1||
Due to his great shame, no joy arose in his heart;
because of that lack of gladness, his mind turned away and could not remain fixed upon his vow.
Although he was dominated by sensual passion and was acting as if in jest,
he did not tolerate those words once the cause had reached its fruition.
And because he had previously considered heaven to be permanent due to his lack of discernment, he now experienced intense agitation upon hearing that it was subject to decay. ||4||
His horse of a resolve, his mental chariot, turned back from heaven, like a great chariot being diverted from a wrong path by a vigilant charioteer. ||5||
Having turned away from the thirst for heaven, he immediately became as if restored to health;
like a sick man wishing to live who has desisted from delicious but unwholesome food.
Just as he had forgotten his beloved wife upon seeing the apsarases,
so too, agitated by the realization of impermanence, did he abandon even the apsarases.
Reflecting that even for great beings there is rebirth,
he became like one free from passion through his sense of urgency, even though he was still possessed by passion.

For that spiritual agitation arose for the sake of his increase in excellence, just as the root *edh* is recited by those who contemplate syllables within the verbal conjugation of the *dhātu-pāṭha*. (9)
But his mind was not captivated by desires by anything;
his steadfastness was held to be like the verb "as" (to be), which occurs in all three tenses. ||10||
Moving with a graceful gait, the mighty-armed one, like a rutless lord of elephants,
approached his preceptor at the proper time, desiring to express his own intention.
Having bowed his head to the guru, his eyes clouded with tears,
he joined his palms in reverence and, with his face slightly cast down in shame, spoke these words.
"O Blessed One, since you have been my guarantor for the attainment of the Apsarases, I have no need for the Apsarases; I renounce your status as my guarantor. (13)
Having heard of the revolving nature of heaven and the diversity of worldly existence,
neither among mortals nor among gods does active engagement appeal to me.
If, having attained heaven through effort, self-restraint, and discipline, they fall at the end still unsatiated, homage to that renouncer for the sake of heaven! 15.
Therefore, having understood the entire world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
I take delight in your supreme Dharma, which brings about the destruction of all suffering.
Therefore, O best of listeners, you should explain that to me both in detail and in summary, so that by hearing it, I may attain the supreme state.
Then, having understood her intention, as well as her faculties and their opposing tendencies, and perceiving that what was beneficial had become manifest before her, the Tathāgata spoke accordingly.
Ah! This reflective discernment is the precursor to your supreme good, rising up like smoke from fire produced by the friction of the kindling wood. (19)
Having wandered for a long time on the wrong path by means of the restless horses of the senses, you have fortunately descended onto the right path through the grace of unclouded vision. (20)
Today your birth has become fruitful, and today you have attained a most great gain, since your mind, though accustomed to the flavor of desire, is now eager for renunciation. (21)
In this world, which delights in the *ālayavijñāna*, joy in cessation is difficult to find;
for the foolish tremble at the prospect of non-rebirth, as if falling from a precipice. (22)
People strive with the thought, "May there be no suffering; may there be happiness for me";
yet they do not understand that true happiness is the absolute cessation of suffering. (23)
The world is attached to desires and the like—which are enemies, impermanent, and constant causes of suffering—and thus does not know the imperishable bliss. 24.
That [remedy] which removes all suffering is indeed the nectar within your hand; for you wish to drink the antidote only after having already drunk the poison at the appointed time. (25)
O you who are worthy of honor, your intended action is unworthy and yet it strikes fear into the cycle of existence;
for such is the fire of passion that it turns one away from the Dharma even when one is intent upon it. (26)
Steadfastness is altogether difficult to maintain with a mind frenzied by passion, just as it is for a thirsty traveler who sees water that is tainted with poison. (27)
Such an intellect of yours has indeed become perverted by passion (rajas), like the radiance of the sun obscured by a fierce wind of dust. ||28||
She who now manifests herself, desiring to destroy the darkness of the heart, is like the solar radiance vomited forth by Mount Meru to dispel the darkness of night. 29.
And this indeed is the fitting state for a mind of pure being:
that it should possess faith in the ultimate, subtle, and supreme good. (30)
Therefore, you ought to increase this desire for the Dharma;
for all phenomena, O Knower of Dharma, are invariably caused by desire. (31)
For when the cognition of going is present, one proceeds to go; likewise, when there is the cognition of lying down, one lies down, and when there is the cognition of standing, one stands. (32)
When a person has faith that water exists within the earth, then, being desirous of it, he digs into this ground with effort. (33)
If one had no need for fire, one would not have faith in it; nor would anyone churn the fire-sticks in its absence, yet when it is absent, they are indeed churned. (34)
If a farmer did not have faith in the growth of crops in the earth, or if he were not desirous of the crop, he would not sow seeds in the ground. (35)
And for this reason, faith has been specifically called "the hand" by me; because, like a hand, it grasps the true Dharma as one's inheritance. (36)

Because of its preeminence it is called a faculty (*indriya*); because of its stability it is called power (*bala*); and because it pacifies the poverty of qualities, it is described as wealth (*dhana*). (37)
It is called *iṣīkā* because it serves for the protection of the Dharma;
and because it is difficult to find in this world, it is designated as a "jewel" (*ratna*). (38)
Furthermore, when she is called "the seed" because she is the cause of spiritual welfare, she is again designated as "the river" in the sense that she purifies evil. (39)
Since faith is the supreme cause for the arising of the Dharma, I have therefore described it in various ways according to its function in different contexts. (40)
Therefore, you ought to nurture this sprout of faith;
for when it grows, Dharma increases, just as a tree does when its roots grow. (41)
He whose vision is confused and whose resolve is weak,
his wavering faith does not lead to the accomplishment of what is to be done.
As long as reality has not been seen or heard, faith does not become firmly established or stable;
but when reality is seen, one whose senses have been subdued by discipline [possesses it].
Faith becomes a tree that is both fruitful and a refuge. ||43||
The twelfth canto, titled "Discernment," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*, is concluded.
The thirteenth canto:
Virtue and Restraint of the Senses.
Then Nanda, having been won over by the great seer regarding faith,
was as if sprinkled with nectar and filled with supreme joy.
The Fully Awakened One considered him as one who had achieved his purpose through that faith; and he, having been refined by the Buddha, considered the highest good as already attained.
That leader disciplined some with gentle words, some with harsh speech, and others with both of these means. (3)
Just as gold, born from dust, is pure, stainless, and clean, and though it remains amidst the dust, it is not defiled by the defects of the dust; ||4||
Just as a lotus leaf, though born in the water and situated in the water, is not defiled by the water either above or below; ||5||
In the same way, a sage born in the world and practicing for the benefit of the world is not defiled by worldly dharmas, because of his perfected nature and his stainless purity. (6)

At the time of reproaching him for the sake of medical treatment, he employed endearment, abandonment, pleasantness, harshness, conversation, and even meditation; yet he did not act out of self-indulgence.
And for this reason, out of that great compassion, he assumed a body, being full of pity [and thinking]: "How might I liberate sentient beings from suffering? (8)
Then, perceiving that Nanda had been gladdened and made a fit vessel,
the best of speakers, who knew the proper sequence of the steps toward the highest good, spoke.
From this time forward, O gentle one, you ought to protect your conduct with faith as your primary guide, for the attainment of the immortal state. (10)
Act so that your application of body and speech becomes pure—open, transparent, guarded, and without flaw. (11)
It is "upturned" (uttāna) because it brings about realization; it is "uncovered" (vivṛta) because it does not conceal [the truth];
it is "guarded" (gupta) through its intentness on protection; and it is "without flaw" (acchidra) because it is irreproachable. ||12||
For the purification of body and speech, as well as in the sevenfold action,
you ought to refine your livelihood and conduct through purity.
By not indulging in the five faults, such as hypocrisy and the rest, and by abandoning the four practices that destroy one's livelihood, such as astrology and the like. ||14||
By not accepting prohibited items such as living beings, grains, and wealth;
and by accepting alms that have been offered, are appropriate for mendicants, and are restricted [in quantity]. ||15||
Contented, pure, and gentle, with a livelihood that is clean and wholesome, one should apply the remedy for suffering only so far as it leads to liberation. (16)

For indeed, because it is difficult to purify, I have taught livelihood as something distinct from action, even though it arises from body and speech just like [other] actions as they are observed. (17)
For the view of a householder with its various perspectives is difficult to purify, and the livelihood of a monk who depends on others for his subsistence is likewise difficult to purify. (18)
This much is declared to be moral conduct; this is the practice in brief.
Through its destruction, there would be neither the state of a renunciant nor that of a householder. (19)
Therefore, endowed with right conduct, practice this celibacy, perceiving danger even in the slightest faults and remaining firm in your vows. (20)
For all actions leading to the highest good proceed by relying upon moral conduct, just as all undertakings depend upon the earth as their foundation. (21)
"O gentle one, let it be understood that detachment is the secret essence of liberation;
the secret essence of detachment is self-awareness, and the secret essence of self-awareness is the vision of knowledge. (22)
Let it be understood that the secret essence of knowledge is indeed meditative concentration (samādhi);
and the secret essence of meditative concentration is physical and mental bliss. (23)
Tranquility is the supreme proximate cause of physical and mental bliss;
let it be understood that joy is likewise the proximate cause of tranquility. //24//
Likewise, joy is considered the secret essence of love; and the absence of remorse regarding deeds well done or ill done is the secret essence of joy. (25)
The pure secret essence of the mind free from mental impressions is moral conduct (*śīla*);
therefore, since moral conduct leads to the highest state, purify your moral conduct. (26)

It is called "śīla" (virtue) because of its being practiced (*śīlana*); practice arises from cultivation (*sevana*); cultivation arises from following instructions (*nideśa*); and instruction arises from taking that [teaching] as one's refuge (*āśraya*). //27//
For morality, O gentle one, is a refuge like a guide in a wilderness;
it is a father, a kinsman, a protection, wealth, and indeed strength. (28)
Therefore, O gentle one, you ought to cultivate ethical discipline;
for this is the foundation, as well as other things, for yogins at the commencement of liberation. (29)
Therefore, establishing yourself in mindfulness, you ought to restrain the senses—which by their very nature are fickle—from the objects of the senses. (30)
One should not fear an enemy, nor fire, nor water, nor lightning as much as one should fear one's own senses; for by them one is constantly destroyed. (31)
Someone may or may not be afflicted by enemies or foes at some time;
however, everyone is oppressed by the sense-faculties everywhere and at all times. (32)
One who is slain by enemies and the like does not go to hell;
however, one who is struck down and rendered helpless by the restless senses is dragged there.
For one being struck by those [weapons], the suffering may or may not be mental;
but for one oppressed by the senses, there is both mental and physical suffering. (34)
For the arrows consisting of the five senses are smeared with the poison of volition;
they have thought for their nock, pleasure for their fruit, and range through the space of the sense-objects. (35)
Driven by the hunter that is desire, they strike human deer in the heart;
if they do not kill them, those deer fall, wounded by them. (36)
Stationed upon the courtyard of self-restraint, wielding the bow of fortitude and clad in the armor of mindfulness, they must be warded off as they fall by that great being.
Due to the tranquility of his senses, as if from the subduing of enemies,
he sleeps or sits happily wherever he goes, free from agitation.
For those who constantly crave sense objects in this world, there is no true awareness due to their wretchedness, just like that of dogs driven by hope. (39)
The collection of sense organs finds no satisfaction through sense objects,
just as the ocean, though being filled incessantly, is never satiated by waters.
In this world, the sense faculties must necessarily function within their respective domains;
however, one should not grasp at the primary signs (*nimitta*) therein, nor even at the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
Having perceived a form with the eye, remaining established in the mere elements, you should not conceptualize it as "a woman" or "a man. (42)
If some grasping at "woman" or "man" were to exist anywhere, you should not pursue the hair, teeth, and so forth as being beautiful. (43)
Nothing is to be removed from that, nor is anything at all to be added;
reality is to be seen as it truly is, exactly as it is, and for what it is. (44)
Thus, as you perceive reality as the constant domain of the senses, it will become a state that is no longer a ground for covetousness or dejection. (45)
Covetousness, under the guise of a pleasing form, destroys the world whose nature is desire, just as an enemy with the face of a friend destroys one who is pure in heart through pleasant speech. (46)
But hostility, which is designated as mental distress, relies upon sense objects;
through its persistence, accompanied by delusion and other factors, one is destroyed both in this world and in the next. (47)
Afflicted by likes and dislikes as if by cold and heat, the world whose senses are restless finds neither comfort nor the highest good. (48)
The sense faculty does not become attached to its object, even though it has engaged with it, as long as conceptual construction of the mind does not operate therein. (49)
Just as fire blazes when there is fuel and wind, so too does the fire of the afflictions arise from sense objects and conceptual construction. (50)
For one is bound by the object through unreal imagination;
seeing that very same object as it truly is, one is completely liberated. ||51||
For upon seeing a single form, one person is filled with passion, another becomes repulsed, someone else remains indifferent, and yet another feels loathing for that very same thing. (52)
Therefore, the object is neither a cause for bondage nor for liberation;
through a particular conceptual construction, there may or may not be attachment. (53)
Therefore, restraint of the senses must be practiced with supreme effort;
for unguarded senses lead to suffering and to continued existence. (54)
For those who enjoy sensual pleasures, whose vision is clouded by the view of a self, whose sole summit is negligence, whose tongues are flickering with excitement,
and who are like serpents of the senses dwelling in the hole of the mind— poisonous with craving— there is no remedy seen for them except the antidote of tranquility.

Therefore, since these enemies that produce unwholesome states—namely the eye, nose, ear, tongue, and body—are to be restrained in every situation, remain vigilant; do not, for even a moment, allow yourself to be negligent in this matter. (56)
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the thirteenth canto, titled “Virtue and the Restraint of the Senses,” is completed.
Canto Thirteen:
Virtue and the Restraint of the Senses.

felt as if sprinkled with nectar and was filled with supreme joy.

That leader disciplined some with gentle words, some with harsh speech, and others with both of these means. (3)

This much is what is called moral conduct; this is the summary of right behavior.

Therefore, endowed with right conduct, practice this celibate life (brahmacarya), perceiving danger even in the slightest faults and remaining firm in your vows. (20)
For all activities leading to the highest good proceed by relying upon morality, just as all tasks such as standing and moving depend upon the earth as their foundation. (21)
