The collection of sense organs finds no satisfaction through sensory objects, just as the ocean, though being filled incessantly, is never satiated by waters. (40)
In this world, the sense-faculties must necessarily operate within their respective domains;
however, one should not grasp at the primary signs (*nimitta*) therein, nor even at the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). //41//
Having perceived a form with the eye, established in the mere element [of vision], you should not conceptualize it as "a woman" or "a man. (42)
If some grasping for "woman" or "man" were to exist anywhere at all, you ought not to pursue the hair, teeth, and so forth as being beautiful. (43)
Nothing is to be removed from that, nor is anything at all to be added;
reality is to be seen as it truly is, in its suchness, and exactly as it is. 44.
Thus, as you perceive reality as the constant domain of the senses,
it will become a state that is no longer a basis for covetousness or dejection.
Covetousness, under the guise of a pleasant form, destroys the world whose nature is desire;
it is like an enemy with the face of a friend, possessing sweet speech but a foul heart. (46)
But hostility, which is designated as mental distress, relies upon sense objects;
by it, when followed by delusion and the rest, one is destroyed both in this world and in the next. (47)
Afflicted by likes and dislikes as if by cold and heat, the world whose senses are restless finds neither comfort nor the highest good. (48)
The sense faculty does not become attached to its object, even though it has engaged with it, as long as conceptual construction of the mind does not operate therein. (49)
Just as fire blazes when there is fuel and wind, so too does the fire of the afflictions arise from sense objects and conceptual construction. (50)
For one is bound by the object through unreal imagination;
seeing that very same object as it truly is, one is completely liberated. ||51||
For upon seeing a single form, one person indeed becomes impassioned, another becomes repulsed, someone else remains indifferent, and yet another feels loathing for that very same thing. (52)
Therefore, the object is neither a cause for bondage nor for liberation;
through a particular conceptual construction, there may or may not be attachment. //53//
Therefore, restraint of the senses must be practiced with the utmost effort;
for unrestrained senses lead to suffering and to continued existence. (54)

By those who enjoy the pleasures of desire, whose vision is the view of a self, whose singular head is heedlessness, whose flickering tongues are their intense joy, and who are serpents of the senses dwelling in the hole of the mind with longing as their venom—nothing has been seen that can cure them except for the medicine of tranquility (śama). //55//

Therefore, regarding these unwholesome enemies—the eyes, nose, ears, tongue, and body—you must remain vigilant at all times through constant restraint; do not, for even a moment, allow yourself to be negligent in this matter. (56)
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the thirteenth canto, titled "Virtue and the Restraint of the Senses," is completed.
Canto Fourteen: The Initial Departure.
Then, having closed the door of the senses with the bolt of mindfulness,
be moderate in eating for the sake of meditation and health.
It suppresses the out-breath and in-breath, brings on exhaustion and sleep, and food taken in excess destroys one's vigor. (2)
Just as food taken in excessive measure leads to misfortune, so too food consumed in too small a measure does not lead to strength. (3)
Food that has been eaten in too small a quantity diminishes one's accumulation [of tissues], luster, enthusiasm, application, and strength as well. (4)
Just as a scale bends down under a heavy load and rises up with a light one, so too does this body remain balanced when provided with appropriate food. (5)
Therefore, observing one's own capacity, one should consume food that is neither excessive nor too small, even if it is measured by conventional standards.
For the bodily fire, when overwhelmed by heavy food, is extinguished, just as a small fire suddenly covered by a great quantity of fuel. //7//
Even a complete cessation of food is not recommended;
for by abstaining from food, one is extinguished like a fire without fuel. (8)
Since there is no subsistence for any living beings without food, therefore food itself is not blameworthy; rather, it is conceptual discrimination that is to be restrained in this regard. //9//
For living beings do not become attached elsewhere to a single object in such a way as they do when food is unknown; the reason for this must be understood therein. (10)
Just as one who has a wound applies an ointment for the sake of healing, so too should food be consumed by one seeking liberation for the sake of warding off hunger. 11.
Just as the axle of a chariot is lubricated for the purpose of bearing a burden, so does the wise man partake of food for the sake of sustaining life. 12.
And for the sake of crossing the wilderness, like two travelers, a husband and wife, though deeply distressed, might eat the flesh of their own son. (13)
In this way, food should be consumed with discernment:
not for the sake of adornment, nor for the sake of the body's appearance, nor for intoxication, nor for pride. (14)
For food is prescribed for the sake of sustaining the body, like a prop for a weak house that is about to fall. (15)
Just as someone might diligently construct and even maintain a raft—not out of attachment to it, but because of the desire to cross over a great flood—so too [should one maintain the body]. (16)
In this way, those who investigate maintain the body with the necessary requisites;
yet it is not out of affection for it, but rather out of a desire to cross over the flood of suffering. (17)
Just as one who is grieving and oppressed gives to an enemy neither out of devotion nor out of desire, but solely for the sake of protecting his life; so too [is this giving]. (18)
In this way, the practitioner of yoga provides food to the body solely for the purpose of warding off hunger, neither out of passion nor for the sake of physical beauty. (19)
And by means of mental concentration, the self-possessed one,
having cast off sleep through yoga, should pass even the night in transformation.
If sleep should manifest in your heart while you still possess consciousness, then do not form within your mind the notion that this is a state characterized by the qualities (guṇas). ||21||
You must always maintain resolve and steadfastness, as well as fortitude and valor in your mind, whenever you are being assailed by sleep. (22)
Those teachings which you have heard should be clearly committed to memory;
they should be taught to others and reflected upon by yourself as well. (23)
One who desires to remain awake should always moisten the face with water, look toward all directions, and direct the gaze toward the stars. 24.
With your senses withdrawn, steady, and under control, and with a mind undistracted, you may either walk about or sit at night. (25)
In fear, in joy, and in sorrow, one is not overcome by sleep;
therefore, when sleepiness assails, these three should be practiced. (26)
You ought to experience fear from the arrival of death, joy from the embrace of dharma, and sorrow from the boundless suffering of birth. (27)
O gentle one, such a sequence of actions should be undertaken for the sake of staying awake; for life becomes fruitless through sleep—what wise man would allow this? (28)
Having transcended the serpents of the faults as if they were snakes within one's own home,
it is not fitting for a wise man who desires to cross over the great danger to sleep.
For while the world of living beings is ablaze with the fires of death, disease, and old age, who could lie down without anxiety, as if in a burning house? (30)
Therefore, knowing it to be darkness, you ought not to embrace sleep while your vices remain unappeased, like enemies still bearing weapons.
Having passed the first watch of the three-watch night through spiritual practice, the independent practitioner should resort to a bed for the sake of resting the body. (32)
Remaining on your right side with the perception of light, you should lie down with a tranquil mind, having brought about awakening within your heart. (33)
And having risen in the third watch of the night, whether walking or sitting, you should once again practice yoga for the purification of the mind with your senses restrained. (34)
Furthermore, regarding sitting, standing, looking, speaking, and so forth, you should maintain mindfulness by being fully aware of all these actions. (35)
Just as enemies cannot assail a well-guarded city, so faults do not overcome him whose mindfulness is stationed at the gateway like a gatekeeper. (36)
Affliction does not arise for one whose mindfulness is directed toward the body;
in all circumstances, it protects the mind like a nurse protects an infant. (37)
But he who is devoid of the armor of mindfulness is a target for faults, like a warrior standing in battle without his armor against his enemies. (38)
That mind should be known as unprotected which mindfulness does not guard, like a leader devoid of sight wandering upon uneven terrain. (39)
Attached to what is harmful and turned away from their own true interests, they are not agitated even when danger arises; in this case, the loss of mindfulness is the cause.
All the virtues, such as ethical discipline and the rest, that abide within their own respective stages—just as a cowherd follows his scattered cows—mindfulness follows after them. (41)
The nectar of immortality is lost for him whose mindfulness has wandered away;
the nectar of immortality is held in his hand by him whose mindfulness is established within his body. (42)
Whence can there be noble method for one who possesses no mindfulness?
And for one who possesses neither nobility nor method, the path of truth is lost. (43)
For him whose path of righteousness is lost, the immortal state is lost;
for him whose immortal state is lost, he is not released from suffering. (44)
Therefore, whether you are moving about or standing still, you should maintain mindfulness in such matters as these. ||45||
O gentle one, resort to a secluded dwelling, free from noise and conducive to yoga;
for having first achieved physical solitude, it is easy to attain mental solitude. (46)

One who has not attained tranquility of mind and is still possessed by passion does not resort to a secluded way of life; for, like one walking upon a path strewn with many thorns, he is harmed because he has not found the Path. (47)

When the investigator has not yet seen the reality and remains amidst the manifold movement of sense objects, it is not easy to restrain the mind, just as a bull that has been dragged away from the midst of the crops [returns] to them. (48)
Just as fire, when not fanned by the wind, comes to rest, so too the mind, when left undisturbed in secluded places, attains peace with little effort. (49)
Having eaten whatever food he finds at any time, and wearing whatever garment he has,

he dwells delighting in the Self; wherever he may be, he takes pleasure in solitude— he who knows the flavor of the bliss of tranquility and whose mind is perfected, should be known as one who has achieved his purpose.
He avoids association with others as if they were thorns. //50//
If, in this world that delights in duality and whose hearts are distracted by sense objects, a wise man of peaceful heart dwells in solitude free from duality;
then, having drunk the essence of wisdom like nectar, his heart is satisfied.
Detached himself, he grieves for the world that is attached and miserable in its pursuit of sense objects. ||51||
If, dwelling in an empty house, he always delights in solitude;
if he takes no pleasure in the arising of afflictions, as if they were enemies;
and if, wandering while delighting in the self, he drinks the water of joy—
Thereafter, he enjoys a supreme happiness even greater than the sovereignty of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Initial Departure," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
Fifteenth Chapter: Abandoning Discursive Thought.
Having assumed the supreme cross-legged posture in a secluded place here or there,
Having straightened the body and being endowed with mindfulness directed toward the front. ||1||
One should make the restless mind devoted to a focal point, whether at the tip of the nose, on the forehead, or indeed between the eyebrows. (2)
If the fever of the mind—discursive thought of sensual desire—should overcome you, it must be cast away and not tolerated, like dust that has settled upon a garment. (3)
Although you have abandoned sensual desires through discernment, destroy them with their antidote, as darkness is dispelled by light. (4)
The latent tendency of those [passions] remains hidden, like fire beneath ashes;
O gentle one, it is to be extinguished by your meditative cultivation, just as fire is quenched by water. (5)
For they proceed from that [cause], just as sprouts arise from a seed;
by the destruction of that [cause], they would not exist, just as sprouts do not exist when the seed is destroyed. ||6||
Having seen that the acquisition of desires and so forth result in suffering for those who crave them,
therefore cut them off at their very root, as one would enemies disguised as friends.
Sensual pleasures are impermanent, deceptive by nature, empty, and causes of calamity; they are common to many and should be discarded like venomous serpents. (8)
Those things which, when sought, lead to suffering; when guarded, do not lead to peace;
when lost, lead to great grief; and even when obtained, do not lead to satisfaction—[these are the objects of the world]. (9)
He who perceives satisfaction through the abundance of wealth, the fulfillment of purpose through the attainment of heaven,
and the arising of happiness from sensual desires, perishes.
You should not dwell here upon those sensual pleasures which are unstable, devoid of essence, unestablished, and whose happiness is merely imagined. (11)
If malice or cruelty should disturb your mind, it must be cleared by its opposite, just as turbid water is clarified by a jewel. (12)
The remedies for these two should be known as loving-kindness (maitrī) and compassion (kāruṇya);
for there is a constant opposition between them, like that of light and darkness. (13)
He whose misconduct has ceased but who still gives way to malice destroys himself with his own dust, like an elephant after a bath. (14)
For what noble person, possessed of compassion, would wish to inflict further suffering upon mortals already afflicted by disease, death, old age, and the like? (15)
Whether another person is harmed here by one's wicked mind or not, the mind of that evil-hearted person is nevertheless consumed by fire immediately. (16)
Therefore, toward all living beings, you should cultivate only loving-kindness and compassion;
you ought not to entertain thoughts of malice or violence. 17.
Whatever a person habitually dwells upon and reflects upon, by that very practice his mind becomes inclined toward it. (18)
Therefore, having abandoned the unwholesome, you ought to meditate on the wholesome, so that it may be for your benefit in this world and for the attainment of the ultimate goal. (19)
For unwholesome thoughts, once accumulated in the heart, increase and produce harm equally for oneself and for others. (20)
By creating obstacles to what is beneficial, they lead to one's own ruin;
and by destroying the state of being a worthy recipient, they lead to the ruin of another's devotion. (21)
Furthermore, you ought to practice non-distraction regarding mental actions;
however, my dear friend, you must never entertain unwholesome thoughts.
Whatever thought concerning the enjoyment of sensual pleasures dwells in the mind, one does not attain that quality [of pleasure], and it only serves to lead to bondage. (23)
Leading to the injury of sentient beings and the affliction of oneself, one falls into delusion and turbidity, and proceeds toward hell. (24)
Therefore, you ought not to destroy yourself with unwholesome thoughts,
like one digging the earth with a fine sword adorned with jewels as if it were mere mud.
Just as one ignorant of the proper method might burn genuine aloe-wood as if it were common firewood, so too does one destroy this human state through unrighteousness. 26.
Just as one might abandon a jewel for a clod of earth and carry it away from an island of jewels,
so too does one abandon the dharma that leads to the highest good and contemplate what is impure.
Just as one might go to the Himalayas and consume poison instead of medicine, so too, having attained human birth, one should practice evil and not what is auspicious. 28.
Having understood this, you ought to cast out discursive thought by means of its antidote, just as one drives out a wedge from within a piece of wood with a finer counter-wedge. (29)

Furthermore, if there should arise anxiety regarding the prosperity or decline of one's kinsmen, the nature of the world of living beings must be examined in order to bring that anxiety to an end. (30)

For sentient beings being dragged through cyclic existence by their own karma, who is a stranger and who is one's own kin? It is only through delusion that a person becomes attached to other people. (31)
For in the past time, people were indeed your own kin;
and in the future time that has not yet arrived, people will become your own kin.
Just as there is a gathering of birds here and there at evening, so too is there a coming together of people and their own kin in birth after birth. (33)
Just as travelers take refuge in various dwellings and then depart, having abandoned them, so too is the meeting with kinsmen. (34)
In this world, which is by nature divided, no one is dear to anyone;
the world is bound together by causes and effects, like a handful of sand. //35//
For the mother nourishes her son with the thought, "She shall support me";
the son honors his mother with the thought, "She bore me in her womb. (36)
When kinsmen behave in a favorable manner toward their kin, they then manifest affection; however, it is the opposite in the case of enmity. (37)
A kinsman may appear as a stranger, and a stranger may appear as a kinsman; people sever and create affection according to their worldly interests. (38)
Just as a painter takes delight in a woman after having painted her himself, so too does one person come to union with another by creating affection oneself. (39)
Those kinsmen who were dear to you in the other world are now performing labor for you, or else you are performing labor for them. (40)
Therefore, you should not entangle your mind with thoughts of kinsmen;
in this cycle of existence, there is no fixed distinction between one's own people and strangers. (41)
"Such-and-such a country is secure, such-and-such is well-supplied with food, and such-and-such is auspicious"—if some such reflection should arise in you, [then listen]. (42)
O gentle one, having realized that the entire world is ablaze with those various fires of defects, you must abandon it; you must not dwell within it in any way whatsoever. (43)
Due to the turning of the wheel of seasons and also from hunger, thirst, and fatigue, suffering is constant everywhere; nowhere is there anything auspicious. (44)
In some places there is cold, in others heat; in some places disease, and in others fear.
These afflict the world excessively; therefore, the world is without refuge. (45)
Old age, disease, and death are the great terrors of this world;
there is no place where these terrors do not occur. (46)
Wherever this body goes, suffering follows there;
there is no destination in the world where one who has gone is not afflicted. (47)
Even a region that is delightful, well-supplied with food, and secure should be known as a "bad country" if one is tormented by afflictions there. (48)
For this world, which is afflicted by physical and mental sufferings, there is no secure place anywhere where one might go and be at ease. (49)
Since suffering exists everywhere, for everyone, and at all times, O gentle one, do not direct your desire and passion toward the variegated wonders of the world. (50)
When your desire and passion for that have ceased, then you will regard the entire world of living beings as if it were ablaze. (51)
Now, if some thought should arise in you that is based on immortality, it must be diligently destroyed, just like a disease located within one's own body. (52)
One must not place trust in life for even a single moment;
for Time, like a lurking tiger, is the slayer of those who are heedless.
"It does not behove you to think, 'I am strong' or 'I am young';
for death strikes in all conditions and does not regard one's age. (54)
For one who perceives the true goal and drags about this body, which is a field for misfortunes, neither hope for health nor hope for life arises. (55)
Who could possibly exist as a body that carries the great elements as its support, like a vessel for waters that are mutually opposed? (56)
One exhales immediately after one inhales;
understand this as a marvel, for life is indeed not to be trusted. (57)
This is another marvel: that one who has slept wakes up, or having risen sleeps again; for embodied beings have many enemies. (58)
Who would place their trust in that Death, who follows the world from the very moment of conception with the intent to destroy it, like one with a raised spear against his enemies? (59)
A person born in this world, though learned and powerful, does not conquer Death;
no one has ever conquered him, nor will anyone ever conquer him.
Whether by conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, force, or restraint,
once impetuous death has arrived, it cannot be repelled.
Therefore, you should not place trust in this flickering life;
for Time constantly carries it away and does not wait for old age.
For one who perceives the world as devoid of essence, like a bubble on water, what person with a sane mind would harbor the thought of immortality? (63)
Therefore, my friend, for the sake of abandoning these discursive thoughts, you ought to take mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation as your object in brief. (64)
By this practice, you should apply yourself at the proper time, as one would use antidotes for diseases to counteract discursive thoughts. (65)

Just as gold-washers, for the sake of gold, first discard the large particles of dust and then, for the sake of its purification, abandon even the subtle ones, having cleansed them, and retain the fragments of gold. (66)

With a mind disciplined for the sake of liberation, having first abandoned the gross faults, he likewise abandons even the subtle ones for the sake of that purification; having cleansed the constituent parts of the factors of existence (dharmas), he attains stability.
Just as a smith here repeatedly heats and hammers gold that has been obscured by dust until it is purified by water,
so too does the practitioner of yoga here skillfully refine [the mind] which is obscured by defects.
Having purified it from the afflictions, he calms the mind and withdraws it. ||68||
Just as a goldsmith brings forth from his own will the pleasure that is the basis for work in various forms of ornamentation,
so too does a monk of pure mind bring forth the power of the superknowledges (abhijñā) under his own control.
It calms the mind as it wishes and impels it wherever it desires. ||69||
The fifteenth canto, titled "The Abandonment of Discursive Thought," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The sixteenth canto: The Noble Truths.

Thus, by means of mental concentration, having gradually eliminated some things and cultivated others, the yogi attains the four meditative absorptions and invariably acquires the five superknowledges. ||1||

The most excellent supernormal powers of many kinds, the comprehension of the mental conduct of others, the long-term recollection of past births, and the two pure divine faculties of hearing and sight. (2)
From this point onward, by means of the examination of reality, he applies his mind toward the destruction of the outflows;
for it is from there that he correctly understands the four truths, beginning with suffering, as the steps [to liberation]. ||3||
This suffering is of the nature of affliction; this is the cause of suffering, being of the nature of its origin;
this is the cessation of suffering, being of the nature of deliverance; and this is the path leading to peace, being of the nature of protection. ||4||
Having thus understood the Noble Truths with wisdom and having correctly penetrated these four, one overcomes all outflows through cultivation; having attained peace, one is not born again. ||5||

Because of the lack of understanding and the lack of penetration regarding these four aspects which constitute reality, the world mounts the swing of saṃsāra, passing from existence to existence and never attaining peace. (6)
Therefore, understand that birth is, in brief, the root of calamities such as old age and the very nature of suffering;
for this birth is indeed the field for all misfortunes, just as the earth is the source of all medicinal herbs. (7)

For that which is the birth of this manifold suffering, along with its physical form and sense faculties—that is the very origin of this bodily mass, and it is the origin of death and disease as well. (8)

Just as food mixed with poison leads to destruction and not to sustenance, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, so too in this world every birth—whether among animals, above, or below—leads only to suffering and not to happiness. (9)
When activity exists, manifold evils such as old age and the like prevail over living beings;
for even when terrible winds blow, trees that have not yet sprouted do not shake.
Just as the wind has its source in space, as fire lies within the womb of the *śamī* tree, and as water dwells within the earth, so too does suffering have its source in the mind and the body. (11)
Just as fluidity is the inherent nature of water, solidity of the earth, mobility of the wind, and constant heat of fire, so too is suffering the inherent nature of both the body and the mind. (12)
When there is a body, there is the suffering of disease, old age, and so forth, as well as hunger, thirst, rain, heat, cold, and the like;
when the mind is dependent on form and accompanied by its continuations, there is the suffering of grief, discontent, anger, fear, and so forth. (13)
Having perceived directly the suffering of birth, know that suffering likewise exists in the past;
and just as that suffering and this present suffering are suffering, understand that suffering in the future is also the same. (14)
For just as the nature of a seed is observed here to be such whether it has already sprouted or is yet to do so, it must be inferred to be the same;
and just as fire is perceived to be hot whether it has already been so or is yet to be so, it remains hot indeed. (15)
O you of noble conduct, wherever the manifestation of name-and-form occurs in accordance with its qualities, there alone is suffering;
for that which is free from it will not become suffering, nor has it ever been so, nor will it ever be. (16)
And for that suffering of worldly existence in the world, the collection of defects such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth is the cause;
neither God, nor primordial matter (*prakṛti*), nor time, nor water, nor inherent nature (*svabhāva*), nor destiny, nor chance is the cause. (17)
And for this reason it should be understood that the world's engagement with objects proceeds from defects;
for those possessed of passion and darkness die, whereas one who is free from passion and darkness is not born again. ||18||
When a particular desire exists, there occurs the application of vehicles, seats, and so forth, in this or that place;
therefore, it should be understood that the birth of living beings occurs in exactly that way by the power of craving. ||19||

Having seen that sentient beings are under the sway of attachment, being exceedingly devoted to their own kind, know that these [afflictions] have been produced by those very same defects through the power of habitual practice. (20)

Just as a distinction arises here in the bases [of the body] due to anger, joy, and so forth, in the very same way, a distinction produced by the afflictions (kleśa) is not of a single form even across successive births. //21//
In a birth where the afflictions (*doṣa*) predominate, a powerful affliction arises; in one who is passionate, intense passion arises;
in one where delusion (*moha*) predominates, there is a preponderance of the power of delusion; and when those afflictions are slight, the resulting affliction is likewise slight. (22)
For one directly perceives what kind of fruit will accrue; from that, one understands the past seed.
And having directly understood the nature of the seed, one anticipates that future fruit. (23)
In whichever births a person's defects have been exhausted through detachment, he is not born in those [births].
Wherever a residue of defects remains for someone, there his rebirth occurs against his will. (24)

O gentle one, having understood that craving and the like are the causes of that manifold birth, cut them off if you desire liberation from suffering; for the cessation of effects results from the destruction of their causes. (25)

Through the exhaustion of suffering and the complete destruction of its cause, realize for yourself the Dharma that is peaceful and auspicious—the cessation of craving, the eternal refuge, the noble, indestructible protection. (26)

That state wherein there is no birth, no old age, no death, no diseases, no association with the unpleasant, no loss of what one desires, and no separation from what is dear—that is the secure, ultimate, and immutable state. (27)

Just as a lamp that has reached its extinction goes neither to the earth nor to the sky, nor to any cardinal direction or intermediate point, but simply attains peace through the exhaustion of its oil; [so too does the Tathāgata]. (28)
Thus, the one who has accomplished his task and attained liberation goes neither to the earth nor to the intermediate space;
he goes to no direction nor to any intermediate quarter, but through the destruction of the afflictions, he attains absolute peace alone. (29)
The path for its attainment is the method consisting of threefold wisdom and twofold tranquility;
it should be cultivated according to rule by the wise one established in the pure morality that has the three [trainings] as its foremost. (30)

Right speech together with right physical action, and a livelihood that is pure according to the rule—these three, when engaged in the practice of conduct, constitute the basis of ethical discipline for the undertaking of karma. (31)

Regarding the truths such as suffering and the rest, there is the noble vision, right reflection, and exertion; these three, engaged in the method of knowledge and based upon wisdom, lead to the complete destruction of the afflictions. (32)
Right mindfulness and right concentration, joined for the sake of attaining truth through reason—these two, engaged in the practice of yoga, rely on tranquility for the mastery of the mind. (33)

Virtue does not allow the sprouts of the afflictions to spread, just as past time does not allow the sprouts of seeds to grow; for when a person's virtue is pure, their faults cannot overcome them, just as those with a sense of shame cannot overcome the mind. (34)
But concentration suppresses the afflictions, just as a mountain [stills] the great torrents of rivers with its force;
for when concentration is established, the faults do not overpower one, like serpents bound by a mantra. (35)
Wisdom, however, destroys all faults without exception, just as a mountain torrent in the rainy season sweeps away the trees on its banks;
once burnt by it, the faults cannot arise again, just as trees cannot grow where they have been consumed by the fire of a thunderbolt. (36)
Having thoroughly penetrated this noble path of eight limbs, which is clear and invincible, one abandons the causes of suffering and the defects, and attains that state of ultimate peace. (37)

In its practice, there are steadfastness and straightforwardness, modesty and heedfulness, solitude, fewness of desires, contentment, lack of attachment, aversion to worldly activities, and patience. (38)
He who understands suffering according to its true nature, as well as its origin and its cessation, attains peace by means of the Noble Path while dwelling together with virtuous friends. (39)
He who, being afflicted by disease, correctly understands the illness, its cause, and its remedy, shall indeed attain health before long when attended by knowledgeable friends. (40)
Therefore, form the perception of a disease regarding the truth of suffering; likewise, form the perception of the cause of disease regarding the defects.
Form the perception of health regarding the truth of cessation, and the perception of medicine regarding the truth of the path. (41)
Therefore, understand that suffering proceeds from active engagement, and recognize the defects that cause it to proceed;
attain cessation through withdrawal, and likewise understand the path that brings about that cessation. ||42||
Therefore, while one's head and clothing are ablaze, one should deliberate with discernment for the sake of awakening to the truth;
for having failed to see the true path, the world has already been burned, is being burned now, and will be burned in the future. (43)
Whenever one perceives that name-and-form is subject to decay, that vision of his is correct;
and seeing correctly, he attains disenchantment, and through the destruction of delight, passion comes to an end. (44)
I declare that through the destruction of both delight and passion, the mind is perfectly liberated;
when the mind is perfectly liberated from those two, there is nothing further to be done. (45)
For one who understands name-and-form according to their own nature, as well as its cause and its cessation, and who truly sees this, I declare the complete destruction of the outflows. (46)

Therefore, my dear friend, having exerted supreme vigor, strive quickly for the complete destruction of the outflows, while specifically examining the elements as suffering, impermanent, and selfless. (47)

For he who understands the six elements—earth, water, fire, and the rest—both in their general nature and by their own specific characteristics, and understands nothing other than them, understands absolute liberation from them. (48)
Furthermore, one who is determined to abandon the afflictions must examine both the proper time and the skillful means;
for practice undertaken at an improper time or through an incorrect method leads to harm rather than to its intended virtues. (49)
If one were to milk a cow that has not yet given birth, one would obtain no milk at all due to milking at the wrong time;
or even if it were the right time, one would not obtain milk if, out of delusion, one were to milk the cow from its horn.
One who desires fire from wet wood will not obtain it even with great effort;
nor does one obtain fire from dry wood by merely throwing it down, if it is done without the proper means. //51//

Having duly examined the place and time, as well as the measure and the means of yoga, and having carefully considered one's own strength and weakness, an effort should be made that is not contrary to these factors. (52)
That sign which was described as "grasping" should not be cultivated when the mind is being uplifted;
for in this way, the mind does not attain tranquility, just like a fire fanned by a strong wind. (53)
When the mind has become agitated, that specific cause which is certain to bring about tranquility is the time for it;
for in this way, the mind attains peace, just as a blazing fire is extinguished by water. (54)
That cause which is certain to bring about tranquility should not be cultivated when the mind is already dissolved [in absorption];
for in this way, the mind sinks into dissolution even further, like a fire of little substance that is not fanned. //55//
That which is a fixed, uplifting sign is the proper time when the mind has fallen into lethargy;
for in that way the mind becomes capable of action, like a dying fire being fed with fuel. (56)
Nor is an attitude of equanimity desired when the mind has fallen into lethargy or is agitated;
for if neglected in such a state, it would produce intense harm, like an untreated disease in a patient. (57)
When the mind has attained equanimity, that is the time for the sign that is fixed upon equanimity;
for in this way, the application becomes effective for its task, like a chariot with well-controlled horses in motion. (58)
Even when the mind is agitated by the surge of passion, the practice of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*) should not be performed;
for one whose nature is passionate becomes deluded by loving-kindness, just as one suffering from a phlegm disorder is further confounded by consuming oily food. (59)
When the mind is agitated by passion, one should attain steadfastness and cultivate the sign of the unattractive;
for one whose nature is dominated by passion thus attains peace, just as one whose nature is dominated by phlegm does by consuming something dry.
When the fault of malice has arisen in the mind, one must not cultivate an unwholesome object;
for to one whose nature is hatred, the unwholesome leads to destruction, just as a sharp medical treatment might to one whose constitution is dominated by bile.
But when the mind is agitated by the fault of malice, loving-kindness should be cultivated by bringing one's own side [of virtue] to bear;
for loving-kindness serves to pacify the hateful nature, just as cooling treatment serves one whose nature is dominated by bile. (62)
When the movement of the mind is bound by delusion, neither loving-kindness nor the meditation on the foul serves as a remedy;
for through those two, one falls into further confusion, just as one who is of a windy nature becomes even more agitated when subjected to something harsh.
When the activity of the mind is characterized by delusion, one should cultivate the dwelling in "this-conditionality" (idampratyayatā);
for when the mind is deluded, this is the path to peace, just as emollient treatment is for a wind-disorder.
Just as a goldsmith here blows upon the gold placed in the mouth of a forge at the right time, sprinkles it with water at the right time, and gradually leaves it alone at the right time; ||65||

For one should heat gold at the proper time while blowing upon it, and one should quench it in water at the improper time; nor should one, by neglecting it, allow it to reach perfect maturity at the wrong time. //66//

One must correctly observe with the mind the proper signs for both exertion and tranquility, as well as for equanimity at the appropriate time; for even effort is destroyed if it is not preceded by the right means.
Thus the Sugata spoke to him concerning both the turning away from what is improper and the proper course;
and further, having understood his various activities, he taught the methods for the abandonment of discursive thought.

Just as a physician prescribes a treatment for the pacification of whichever humor—bile, phlegm, or wind—has become provoked, so too did the Buddha prescribe a remedy for each of the defilements. (69)

If one does not eliminate unwholesome thoughts through a single eon because they have become so thoroughly habitual, then one should undertake a second successive effort; for a virtuous application must never be abandoned. (70)

Because the multitude of afflictions has accumulated over beginningless time and is thus exceedingly powerful, and because correct application is difficult to achieve, these defects cannot indeed be severed all at once. (71)
Just as a man skilled in such matters removes a large splinter by means of another, smaller splinter, so too should one cast away that very unwholesome mental sign by resorting to another sign. (72)

Nevertheless, if unwholesome thought does not subside because one is still a novice in inner self-mastery, it must be abandoned by examining its faults, just as a traveler avoids a path infested with wild beasts. (73)
Just as one afflicted by hunger, desiring to live, does not wish to eat food mixed with something disagreeable,
so too the wise man, realizing it brings harm, abandons an inauspicious omen.
For who is able to restrain one who does not perceive a fault as a fault?
And he who perceives a virtue as a virtue in whatever it may be, proceeds toward it even when being restrained. (75)
For those born of noble lineage feel shame when unwholesome mental activities proceed;
just as a wise, handsome youth feels constrained by impure, lingering glances fixed upon his neck. (76)

If unwholesome thoughts should persist even in the slightest degree despite being shaken off, one should employ other activities such as study and ritual practice as a method to cause them to be forgotten. (77)
Even sleep must be undertaken with discernment, or even physical exhaustion may be endured;
but one should never intentionally contemplate an improper object, for through attachment to it, misfortune would arise. (78)

For just as one who is afraid of thieves at night would not wish to open his door even to loved ones, so the wise man withdraws his engagement from faults, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious. (79)
If, even when being restrained by such means as these, they do not turn back, then they should be eliminated like defects in gold by removing the grosser portions. ||80||

Just as a man, weary of the harsh application of sensual pleasures beginning with rapid journeys, seeks refuge [in tranquility], so too should the wise man conduct himself even amidst the faults [of the world]. (81)

If those unwholesome thoughts should not be stilled because their antidotes have not been attained, they must not be tolerated for even a moment, like serpents in the house that remain unchecked. (82)
Even by pressing tooth against tooth, or by pressing the tip of the tongue against the palate, and even by seizing the mind with the mind, you must exert effort; for they will not follow your lead.
What is surprising in this, if one who is free from delusion and has gone to the forest should remain composed in mind and not be bewildered?
He who, though being assailed in his heart by the causes of that [delusion], is not shaken—he is the one who has achieved his goal; he is the steadfast man. (84)

Therefore, in order to realize the Noble Truths, first purify the path by this method, just as a king who has set out on a journey desires to conquer unconquered fortune for the sake of subduing his enemies. (85)
These auspicious forests all around are conducive to yoga and undisturbed by people;
having attained mere physical seclusion, devote yourself to the path for the abandonment of the afflictions. (86)
Kauṇḍinya, Nanda, Kṛmila, Aniruddha, Tiṣya, Upasena, Vimala, and Rādha; Bāṣpa, Uttara, Dhautaki, Moharāja, Kātyāyana, Dravya, and Pilindavatsa. (87)
Bhaddāli, Bhadrāyaṇa, Sarpadāsa, Subhūti, Godatta, Sujāta, Vatsa;
Saṃgrāmajit, Bhadrajit, Aśvajit; Śroṇa, Śoṇa, and Koṭikarṇa. ||88||
Kṣema, Ajita, Nandana, Nanda, Mātṛ, Upāli, Vāgīśa, Yaśas, Yaśodā, Mahāhvaya, Valkalin, Rāṣṭrapāla, Sudarśana, Svāgata, and Medhika. (89)
He was Kapphiṇa, Kāśyapa, Auruvelva, Mahā-Kāśyapa, Tiṣya, and Ānanda;
Pūrṇa, Pūrṇa, and that Pūrṇaka, as well as Śoṇa-Parānta—that very Pūrṇa. ||90||
Śāradvatīputra, Subāhu, Cunda, Kondeya, Kāpya, Bhṛgu, Kuṇṭha, Dhāna, along with Śaivala, the two Revata and Kauṣṭhila, he of the Maudgalya lineage, and Gavāmpati. ||91||
Perform quickly and according to the rules that very same valor which you formerly displayed in the practice of yoga;
then you will surely attain the station reached by them, as well as glory encompassed by happiness. (92)

Just as a substance may be pungent by its taste yet sweet when consumed in its digestion, so too is his vigor pungent through exertion, yet its result is sweet for the accomplishment of his purpose. (93)
For energy is the supreme root in the accomplishment of tasks; without energy, there is no success whatsoever.
From energy arises every prosperity in this world, while the absence of energy results in every form of evil. (94)
The failure to obtain what has not been gained, the inevitable loss of what has already been obtained, self-contempt, the miserable humiliation at the hands of superiors,
darkness, lack of luster, and the cessation of learning, discipline, and contentment— [these are the fruits of such a state].
For men who lack vigor, there occurs both downfall and ruin. ||95||
Having heard this method, he is unable to attain further growth;
having known the supreme Dharma, he does not find a higher dwelling;
and having abandoned the home for liberation, he does not find peace.
In this matter, the cause for a person is laziness; it is not an external enemy. ||96||
If one digs the earth with undiminished vigor, one finds water;
by continuously rubbing the fire-drills together, one produces fire.
Indeed, those who apply themselves to yoga certainly obtain the fruit of their exertion.
For rivers, flowing swiftly and constantly, indeed break even through mountains. ||97||
Having ploughed the earth and protected it through hundreds of labors, one enjoys the glory of the harvest;
having diligently plunged into the waters of the ocean, one sports with the glory of jewels;
and having struck down the prowess of enemies with arrows, one enjoys the sovereignty of a lord of men.
Exert that energy for the sake of peace; for when energy is disciplined, all supernatural powers arise. ||98||
The sixteenth canto, titled "The Noble Truths," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The seventeenth canto: "Attaining the Immortal."

Then Nanda, having been thus instructed in the path of reality and having attained the path of liberation, bowed down with his whole being to the Teacher and went to the forest to abandon the afflictions. ||1||
There he saw a peaceful clearing, carpeted with soft, blue-green grass and surrounded by groves of trees;
it was embraced by a silent river flowing with water as blue as lapis lazuli.
Having performed the purification of his feet there at the base of a pure, auspicious, and glorious tree,
he girded his loins with the resolve for liberation and assumed the cross-legged posture, holding it firmly upon his lap.
Having set his body straight and composed, having directed mindfulness toward the body,
and having withdrawn all his senses within himself, he applied himself there with diligent effort to yoga.

Then, desiring to practice the entirety of reality and wishing to perform the rites conducive to liberation, he moved within the field for the cultivation of the mind through knowledge, virtuous conduct, and tranquility. (5)
Having summoned fortitude, applied energy, cast off attachment,
and grasped his own power, he became tranquil in mind, established in self-restraint, composed, and indifferent toward sense objects.
Although his intellect was disciplined and his self was resolutely directed toward renunciation, the notion of sensual desire, due to its long-standing habituation,
threw his mind into confusion— just as lightning and rain agitate the waters during the monsoon season.
Perceiving that obsession, the wise man immediately cast off her who was obstructing his dharma—
just as a man of noble mind, his heart overwhelmed by anger, casts off even a beloved woman whose virtues have become perverse.
But as he exerted his vigor for the sake of mental tranquility, an unwholesome thought arose once more, like a terrible affliction befalling one who is intent on destroying a disease. (9)
To counteract that, he resorted to another auspicious means conducive to yoga,
like a weak man, being driven away by a stronger enemy, takes to a path of distress to escape his foe.

Just as a king, having established his capital, applied punishment, gathered allies, and subdued enemies, attains previously unknown lands, so too is this the policy for one who desires liberation in the practice of yoga. (11)

For even for the yogi who desires liberation, the mind is the city, the method of knowledge is the staff, virtues are the allies, and faults are the enemies; he strives for that purpose which is liberation, the ground. 12.
Desiring to be liberated from the great web of suffering and seeking to enter upon the attainment of the path to liberation,
he went toward tranquility with his eyes somewhat opened, wishing to behold the supreme path that leads to the deathless.
He who would be a dwelling place for darkness is homeless; even after hearing the truth, he remains heedless.
But because he is a fit vessel for liberation, he withdrew his mind into his own self. (14)

Then the self-possessed one duly performed an investigation into phenomena according to their equipment, conditions, intrinsic nature, gratification, specific defects, and the nature of their transcendence. (15)
Desiring to see the essence of both the material and the immaterial, he scrutinized the body;
then he scrutinized the body as impure, suffering, impermanent, non-self, and indeed devoid of a self.
For by means of that preeminent worldly path, he caused the tree of the afflictions to tremble through its impermanence, its emptiness, its selflessness, and its very suffering. (17)
Since everything here comes into being after not having existed, and having existed, it necessarily ceases to exist again;
and since it is caused, subject to decay, and possesses a cause, he therefore concluded that the world is impermanent. (18)

Since for one who is born, the engagement with action—which is the cause of both bondage and its destruction—is necessarily attached to what is called "pleasure" in the form of a remedy for suffering, he therefore perceived worldly existence itself to be suffering. (19)

And since that which belongs to the conditioned is solitary, with no agent or experiencer whatsoever, and since its activity arises from a causal complex, he therefore beheld this world as empty. (20)

Because the world is inactive and lacks autonomy, and no single being exercises sovereignty over actions, he understood that phenomena arise in dependence upon various conditions; therefore, he realized the world to be selfless. (21)
Then, like one fanning for wind on a hot day, or producing fire from wood by friction,
or digging for water hidden within the earth, he attained that world-transcending path so difficult to reach.

Having strung the bow of right knowledge and donned the armor of mindfulness, standing upon the vehicle of pure moral conduct and vows, he stood ready for battle to achieve victory, desiring to fight against the enemies of the afflictions stationed on the battlefield of the mind. (23)

Then, having taken up the sharp weapons of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), mounted upon the supreme vehicle of the right efforts (*samyak-pradhāna*), and accompanied by a force consisting of the elephants of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*), he gradually advanced against the army of the afflictions (*kleśa*). (24)

With arrows consisting of the applications of mindfulness, he instantly shattered his enemies—the four causes of suffering—which consist of the perversions, by means of their respective four bases of activity. (25)
With those five incomparable noble powers, he shattered the five mental wastelands;
likewise, with those eight noble elephants, he utterly routed the eight elephants of false views.

Then, having shaken off every view of a self and being free from doubt regarding the four truths, he—possessing pure conduct, vows, and vision of the Dharma—attained the first stage of the fruit of the Dharma. (27)

Because of the vision of the four noble truths and the dissociation from a portion of the afflictions, and because of the attainment of individual excellence and the direct perception of the bliss of the wise, [he is called a noble one]. ||28||

Due to the firmness of his faith, the stability of his fortitude, his lack of delusion regarding the Four Truths, and the flawlessness of his supreme conduct, he became free from doubt concerning the practice of the Dharma. (29)
Freed from the net of false views and beholding the world as it truly is, he attained a joy rooted in knowledge and once more reached a state of serene confidence toward his teacher. (30)
For he who understands that the process of existence is determined— neither by another cause nor without a cause—
and understands each thing as it arises in dependence upon this or that, he beholds the ultimate, noble Dharma.

He who perceives the Dharma—peaceful, auspicious, ageless, dispassionate, and the supreme good—and then beholds its teacher, the most excellent of noble ones, the Buddha who has attained the eye of wisdom, [attains liberation]. (32)

Just as one who has been freed from disease by the instruction of a benevolent physician looks upon that physician with a mind full of gratitude, so too does one who is liberated look upon the Teacher with the vision of the mind, satisfied by both loving-kindness and the knowledge of the scriptures. (33)

Likewise, one who knows reality and has attained the noble path is liberated; realizing the noble reality, the body-witness beholds the Tathāgata while recollecting him, and he is satisfied by loving-kindness and omniscience. //34//

Freed from destructive views and having perceived the limit of renewed existence, he cast off all aversion toward the manifestations of the afflictions; he feared neither death nor the miserable realms. (35)
Filled with a collection of impurities such as skin, sinews, fat, blood, bone, flesh, hair,
and so forth, he then, closely examining that body and reflecting upon its essence, did not find even an atom of it.
Firm in soul, he thinned both sensual desire and aversion by that very yoga;
having made those two thin upon his broad-chested body, he attained the second fruit in the noble Dharma.

With the weapons of yoga and the arrows of the foul, he shattered the bow of greed, the arrow of conceptual construction, and the great enemy passion—which had been reduced to its last remnants—by means of his realizations regarding the true nature of the body. (38)

He struck down that enemy—whose weapon was hatred, whose scattered arrows were anger, and whose internal offspring was malice—with shafts of loving-kindness stored in the quiver of fortitude, released from the bowstring of patience. (39)
Then the Hero severed the three roots of evil with the three bases of liberation,
just as one standing at the head of an army might strike down three bowmen with three iron-tipped arrows.

Having overcome those who held him back as he sought to transcend the realm of desire, and having attained the fruit of the non-returner through yoga, he stood like the gateway to the city of Nirvana. (41)

Then he attained the first dhyāna, which is secluded from sensual desires and from defiled states, accompanied by applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), and endowed with the joy and happiness born of seclusion. ||42||

Released from the burning fire of desire, he attained supreme joy through the bliss of meditative concentration; like one exhausted by the heat plunging into water, or a pauper obtaining vast wealth. ||43||

There too, having recognized that those thoughts directed toward worldly phenomena and those reflections extended toward merits and faults were unpeaceful and agitated the mind, he resolved to be free from them. (44)

Just as waves cause agitation in the ocean which carries deep and serene waters, so too do discursive thoughts, acting like waves upon the water of the mind, cause agitation in that which has become one-pointed. (45)
Just as sounds cause distress to one who is weary, asleep, or at rest, so too do discursive thoughts cause affliction to one who has now attained one-pointedness of mind. (46)

Then, through one-pointedness of mind, he meditated upon that second dhyāna—tranquil, free from applied thought and sustained reflection, born of concentration, characterized by joy and bliss, and inwardly auspicious. (47)
Having attained that meditation, he achieved mental silence and experienced a supreme joy never before obtained;
yet, even in that joy, he perceived its defects just as he had done regarding discursive thoughts.
For wherever one has supreme delight in an object, there indeed arises suffering from its opposite;
therefore, perceiving the defects therein, he ascended to the yoga that brings about the cessation of delight. (49)

Then, through detachment from joy, experiencing with the body that bliss which is cherished by the noble ones, mindful and clearly conscious, the steadfast one dwelt having attained the third dhyāna, being equanimous. (50)

Because there is no bliss beyond that, and because there is no further progression of bliss superior to it, he who knows the higher and the lower spoke of the stage of the Śubhakṛtsna gods as "supreme" out of loving-kindness. (51)
Then, even in that meditative absorption, he perceived a fault; he considered it to be merely supreme peace and immobility.
Even through its intense application, his mind was overcome by the fact that it had proceeded toward pleasure without effort. (52)
Wherever there is agitation, there is vibration; and wherever there is vibration, there is suffering.
Therefore, because it is characterized by agitation, those ascetics who desire peace abandon that which is pleasant.

Then, through the prior abandonment of pleasure and pain as well as mental fluctuation, there arises the fourth dhyāna, which is characterized by equanimity and mindfulness, and is pure, being neither painful nor pleasant. (54)

But because there is neither pleasure nor pain therein, and because knowledge exists there, acting for its sake, therefore "purity of equanimity and mindfulness" is defined in the procedure for the fourth dhyāna. //55//
Relying upon that fourth dhyāna, he then set his mind on attaining arhatship, just as a king, having secured a powerful and noble ally, desires to conquer unconquered territories. (56)
Then, impelled by his cultivation, he completely severed with the sword of wisdom those five higher fetters, the supreme bonds, the yokes that lead upward. (57)
With the seven elephants of the factors of enlightenment, he likewise crushed the seven latent tendencies of the mind,
just as Time, with its seven planets, destroys the seven continents when their destruction is imminent.

For Nanda applied that same mode of behavior toward his faults which belongs to fire, trees, clarified butter, and water toward a headless trunk, wind, fire, and the sun—by means of extinguishing, uprooting, burning, and drying. (59)

Thus, by means of a raft possessing eight components, he crossed over the difficult-to-traverse ocean of suffering—which has three currents, three crocodiles, three whirlpools, a single body of water, five speeds, two shores, and two sharks. (60)

Having attained arhatship, he became worthy of honor—free from longing, free from attachment, and free from hope; fearless, undismayed, devoid of pride, and dispassionate, he appeared as if someone else through his steadfastness. (61)
Through that instruction of his brother and teacher, and by his own prowess, Nanda then—his mind calmed and his task accomplished—spoke these words to himself: (62)
Homage be to that Sugata, who, desiring my welfare and being the very embodiment of compassion, has turned back many sufferings and bestowed abundant happiness. (63)
For I, being dragged along the path consisting of suffering by ignoble passion born of the body, have been turned back by the goad of his words, like a proud elephant by a hook. (64)

By the command of that compassionate Teacher, having indeed extracted the thorn of passion from my heart, there is already such great happiness for me this very day; how much more so when all [defilements] are destroyed and I am liberated! (65)
Having extinguished the blazing fire of desire with the water of fortitude, as one might quench a fire with water,
I have now attained supreme joy, like a person entering a cool lake during the heat.
Nothing is dear to me, nor is anything undear; I have no attachment, so how could there be aversion?
Due to the absence of both, I am instantly happy, like one released from cold and heat. (67)
As if attaining safety from a great danger, as if obtaining release from a massive prison,
as if reaching the far shore of a vast ocean without a boat, and as if finding light after a terrifying darkness.
Just as health from disease, freedom from debt from a burdensome loan, escape from the presence of an enemy, and abundance from the onset of famine—each being of infinite measure. (69)
In the same way, I have attained supreme peace through the power of that Vināyaka;
once again, I offer repeated salutations to him, the Arhat, the Tathāgata. (70)

By him I was led to the golden-peaked mountain and to heaven, where, through the example of the wives of the monkeys, I—who am possessed by desire and submerged in this age of Kali consisting of young women—was drawn out by celestial damsels. (71)

Therefore, having been pulled out from that mire of misfortune by one devoted to [the Dharma], like an elephant with loosened limbs from the mud, he is liberated in this true Dharma—tranquil, stainless, free from fever, free from grief, free from darkness, and leading to the ultimate goal. (72)
I bow my head to that Great Seer, the supremely compassionate one, who knows the nature of qualities and understands the disposition of beings;
to the Fully Awakened One, possessed of the ten powers, the foremost of physicians—I bow once again to him, the Protector. (73)
The seventeenth canto, titled "The Attainment of Immortality," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is concluded.
The eighteenth canto: "The Prophecy."

Then Nanda, having achieved his purpose, approached his teacher like a twice-born man who has mastered the Vedas as a youth, like a merchant who has swiftly gained a great profit, or like a king who has conquered an enemy army. ||1||

At the time of the completion of his knowledge, it was indeed a joy for the disciple to see the guru, and for the guru to see the disciple; for [the sage] desired to see him, thinking, "Your exertion toward me has borne fruit. (2)
For he by whom excellence has been attained deserves to perform the highest honor for his teacher;
how much more so an Arya who, though still possessed of passion, is free from pride due to his sense of gratitude—let alone one who is free from passion? (3)
For one whose devotion arises from wealth and desire, that devotion remains firmly rooted;
but for one whose passionate devotion follows the path of dharma, his grace penetrates deep into the heart. (4)
Then, clad in saffron robes and radiant as gold, he bowed his head to the Guru,
like a *karṇikāra* tree with the copper-red glow of its sprouts stirred by the wind and the brilliant beauty of its flowers.

Then, for the sake of demonstrating his own qualities as a disciple, the qualities of the Great Sage as a teacher, and the qualities of the Teacher himself, he recounted the accomplishment of his task—not out of pride. (6)

O Lord, that extremely sharp shaft of false views which had deeply pierced my heart and tormented me intensely has been extracted by the pincers of your words, like a splinter removed by one skilled in extracting splinters. (7)
I have reached a state free from doubt, for that uncertainty of mine has been severed;
through your teaching, I have come to the true path, like one who had lost his way finding a good guide. (8)

That poison of Kandarpa which I had drunk out of pride with my senses under the sway of passion has been destroyed by the medicine of your words, just as a deadly poison is neutralized by a great antidote.
Birth has come to an end; I am one whose birth is cast away. I have dwelt perfectly in the practice of the true Dharma.
Everything that was to be done has been done by me; my task is accomplished. I am a being among the worlds, yet I am not subject to worldly dharmas.

O Supreme One, like a calf parched with thirst, I have been thoroughly satiated by drinking from your cow—whose udders are loving-kindness, whose beautiful dewlap is the secondary marks, whose milk is the True Dharma, and whose horns are eloquence. (11)
O Sage, understand from me in brief this realization which has come to me as I see;
O Omniscient One, although this is surely known to you, I wish to explain it according to my own perspective. (12)

For other virtuous people who desire liberation, having heard the method for liberation from another, strive happily by that very same path—just as those afflicted by disease do upon hearing of one who has been freed from illness. ||13||
In this birth, I do not perceive the earth and other elements as the altar, nor do I perceive myself as anything within those elements such as the earth;
therefore, I have no attachment to them, and my mind is equal toward both the external world and the body.

Since I perceive the five aggregates, beginning with form, as flickering and devoid of essence, as well as being selfless and subject to destruction, I am therefore liberated from these inauspicious things. (15)

And because I perceive the arising and passing away of the sense faculties in all their states, therefore I have no attachment even toward them, for they are impermanent, devoid of self, and suffering. (16)
Since I see the world as established in rebirth, entirely essence-less and unreal, therefore my mind is bound by my intellect; there is no longer any agitation in me by which [I might be moved]. (17)
Since I am unattached to the fourfold variety of food and its manifold applications, being neither infatuated nor bound by it, I am therefore liberated from the three states of existence. ||18||

Since my mind is neither fixed nor obstructed regarding the phenomena of worldly convention—such as what is seen or heard—and since it follows the nature of equanimity therein, I have therefore attained dissociation and am liberated. (19)
Having spoken thus, out of great reverence for his teacher, he prostrated himself upon the earth with his entire body;
smeared with red sandalwood paste, he shone like a great golden pillar set in motion.

Then, having heard of his former steadfastness and his prophetic declaration, as well as his serene faith following from the sequence of the Dharma, the Sage with the voice of a cloud addressed him who had previously strayed through negligence: meghastanitanirghoṣaḥ sa munirmeghadurdinaiḥ | meghasvaragabhīreṇa svareṇedamuvāca ha ||22|| With a voice deep as the thundering roar of clouds, that Sage, amidst the overcast skies of rain-clouds, spoke these words in a tone as profound as the sound of a cloud.
"Arise, you who stand firm in the Dharma cherished by disciples! Why have you fallen at my feet with your head?
To me, prostration is not such a mark of worship as this very practice of the Dharma. (22)
Today you have truly gone forth as a renunciant, O self-conqueror, by whom even sovereignty over the self has been attained;
for the life of a renunciant is excellent for one who has conquered the self, but not for one of fickle mind whose senses are unsubdued.
Today you are endowed with supreme purity, for your speech, body, and mind are pure.
Therefore, O gentle one, you shall not again behold that unclean and loathsome bed of the womb.
Having today heard that which is heard in accordance with the sacred revelation, and having understood the Dharma as it conforms to that revelation,
one who has completed his studies yet acts contrary to it is indeed censurable, like a powerless man who has taken up a weapon.
Oh, how great is your fortitude, you whose nature is beyond the sensory realm, that you have set your mind upon the method for liberation!
For it is only the fool who, thinking "I shall reach the ultimate state," succumbs here to fear at the prospect of the destruction of birth. (26)
By good fortune, this rare convergence of conditions has not been rendered fruitless through the power of delusion;
for having sunk down, one rises up with great difficulty, like a turtle in the ocean encountering the opening of a yoke. (27)
Having conquered Māra, who is difficult to resist in battle, you are today the hero at the head of the fray in this world.
For even one who is a hero should be known as no hero if he is struck down by his own faults, just as one is slain by enemies. (28)
Having extinguished the fierce fire of passion today, by good fortune you shall sleep happily, free from burning;
for one whose mind is consumed by the fire of afflictions sleeps in misery, even upon a magnificent bed. (29)
Previously you were exalted by the intoxication of wealth, but today you are truly prosperous through the cessation of craving.
For as long as a person in this world possesses craving, they remain always poor, even if they are wealthy. (30)
"It is now appropriate for you to declare, 'King Śuddhodana is my father';
for when one has fallen from the Dharma due to the downfall brought about by one's ancestors, a claim to noble lineage is indeed not to be praised. (31)
By good fortune you have attained supreme peace, like one who has reached the further shore after crossing a wilderness and secured its essence;
for everyone caught in the cycle of existence is afflicted by fear, just as one who has entered a wilderness.
"When shall I see Nanda dwelling in the forest, subsisting on alms, humble, and composed?
Such was my desire to behold you before; thus it is by good fortune that you have become visible to me. (33)
For even one who is formless becomes beautiful when well-adorned with his own most excellent qualities;
yet one who is surrounded by defiling faults is truly ugly, even if he is handsome to behold. (34)
Today your intelligence has been proven supreme, for by it you have accomplished your entire purpose.
For even one exalted by learning lacks true wisdom if his intellect does not arise toward that which is beneficial. (35)
Even among people with open eyes, the eye of one who lacks the eye consisting of wisdom remains as if closed; for even though he possesses physical sight, he has no true vision. (36)

Afflicted by the need to counteract suffering, the world undergoes exhaustion through agriculture and other labors; yet that suffering returns incessantly and even increases—until today its end has been brought about by you through wisdom. (37)
"The world constantly exerts itself, thinking, 'May I not have suffering; may I have only happiness.
Yet it does not know how that might truly come to pass, as you have today attained that which is so difficult to find. (38)

Thus, for his welfare, the Tathāgata spoke these and other words to him whose intellect and mind were steadfast; and Nanda, indifferent to both praise and blame, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence: (39)

Oh, O Seer of Distinctions, you have shown me this special compassion, in that I, O Blessed One, though submerged in the mire of desire, have been rescued from the fear of saṃsāra without any longing of my own! (40)

If I had not been rescued by you—my brother, my guide to the highest good, my father established in the fruit [of liberation], and likewise my mother—I would have perished like one who has strayed from a caravan, having failed to achieve his purpose. (41)
For one who is peaceful and contented, solitude is happiness; for the investigator who has realized reality, it is happiness;
and for one whose pride is abandoned and who is free from intoxication, detachment is the happiness of one whose intellect is unattached. (42)

For now that I have thoroughly understood reality, completely shaken off my faults, and attained peace, I am intent only upon my own hermitage; I think of neither those people, nor the apsarases, nor the gods.
Having indeed tasted this pure happiness born of tranquility, my mind no longer yearns for pleasure born of desire;
it is like a celestial being who, having consumed nectar, has no further longing for even the most costly food not brought by the gods. (44)
Alas! The world, its vision blinded by ignorance, does not perceive the supreme happiness behind the veil;
for, casting aside the profound bliss of the self, it instead pursues the toil of sensual pleasure. (45)
For just as a foolish person, having come to a mine of jewels, might discard the gems and carry away worthless stones;
so too, casting aside the supreme bliss of perfect enlightenment, one would exert effort for the sake of attaining the pleasure of sensual desires. (46)
Oh, how supreme is the Tathāgata’s desire to favor sentient beings with a mind of exceeding loving-kindness!
For, O Sage, casting aside the highest bliss of meditative absorption, you exert yourself for the sake of ending the suffering of others. (47)

How indeed can I possibly repay you today, my teacher, who desires my welfare and is compassionate toward me—you by whom I have been rescued from the ocean of existence, like one whose ship was shattered by the waves of the great sea? (48)

Then the minister, having heard his reasoned speech which indicated that all taints had been abandoned, spoke these words—the unsurpassed speech of those who speak—which only one who is a mass of glory is worthy to utter: (49)
O wise one, you alone, having accomplished your purpose and knowing the ultimate truth, ought to explain this;
like a great merchant who has crossed the wilderness and attained his goal, you have fulfilled the task for your excellent guide.

Just as an accomplished Arhat with a tranquil mind perceives the Buddha, the charioteer who tames men, so too does an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) not perceive him—even one who has seen the Truth—let alone one who is merely intelligent. //51//
This gratitude of yours is truly worthy of one whose mind is entirely liberated from passion and darkness;
for in this world, O grateful one, which exists in a state of intense passion, a sense of gratitude is indeed rare to find.

Since you possess the true Dharma through its conformity with the Dharma, and since you have both faith toward me and skill in realization, I have much more that I wish to say to you; for one who is humble and devoted deserves to be commanded. (53)
You have accomplished your task and attained the supreme goal; there is not even the slightest thing remaining for you to do.
Therefore, O gentle one, from this point forward, act out of compassion, liberating others who have fallen into distress.

For this very purpose, the base man undertakes action; the mediocre man, however, undertakes action pertaining to both worlds; the middling man undertakes action for the sake of fruit in the world beyond; but the one of distinguished dharma acts again for the sake of non-activity [in future births]. (55)

But among these, he is considered the most excellent even than the most excellent, who, having attained the supreme and final dharma, desires to teach tranquility to others without regarding the personal hardship involved. (56)
Therefore, O steadfast one, setting aside your own affairs here, you should also attend to the affairs of others;
while sentient beings wander with their minds shrouded in darkness, let this lamp of sacred learning be held aloft in the night. (57)
Let the astonished people in the city say, while you stand there delivering teachings on the Dharma:
"Oh, how wonderful! Even this one who is still possessed by passion delivers such discourse for the sake of liberation! (58)
For having heard your firm resolve, her mind will surely turn away from various worldly desires;
and that bride in your house, emulating you, will speak among women of stories that inspire detachment from women.

Established in you, who possess supreme fortitude and have realized the ultimate truth, she will certainly find no pleasure in the life of a householder—just as the discerning mind finds no delight in sensual pleasures when it is secluded and characterized by tranquility and self-restraint. (60)

Thus, having bowed his head and simultaneously grasped both the words and the feet of the Arhat, the supremely compassionate Teacher, he departed from the side of the Sage—composed, with a tranquil heart, his task accomplished, and free from pride like an elephant. (61)
At the proper time, he entered the city for alms, captivating the eyes of the people;
equal toward gain and loss, pleasure and pain, and other such things, his senses composed and free from desire,
he delivered a discourse on liberation to those who sought it at that time.
Neither disparaging others who have gone astray, nor exalting oneself. ||62||

Thus, this work, which contains the essence of liberation, has been composed as a means for listeners to grasp [the truth] through the artifice of poetry, for the sake of tranquility and not for pleasure;
for whatever else I have produced here other than liberation, that was done according to the conventions of poetry.
"How might it be made pleasant to the heart, like bitter medicine mixed with honey, so that one would wish to drink it? ||63||
Having observed that the world for the most part is intent on sensual pleasures and averse to liberation,
I have here related the truth under the guise of poetry, [asserting] that "liberation is supreme.
Having understood this, one should attentively grasp from it that which pertains to tranquility, and not what is merely elegant.
From dust born of the elements, gold as a useful object necessarily arises. ||64||
The eighteenth canto, titled “The Declaration of Knowledge,” in the epic poem *Saundarananda*, is completed.
